courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: How Jamba, Nemotron-H and Qwen3-Next stack their layers
question: Why does Nemotron-H place a Mamba-2 layer first and use no RoPE in its attention layers?
options: RoPE is incompatible with grouped-query attention
The first Mamba-2 layer is recurrent and naturally encodes position, so explicit position embeddings are not needed
Attention layers at the start would make the KV cache grow quadratically
Mamba-2 layers require RoPE inputs and must come before attention
explain: Waleffe et al. put a Mamba layer at the start so the hybrid can work without position embeddings, since the recurrence itself depends on order. Their 840M ablation also found the no-RoPE hybrid did better after long-context extension.

courseTitle: Hybrid search: fusing BM25 and dense retrieval
lessonTitle: A cross-encoder reranks the fused shortlist
question: Your hybrid pipeline reranks the top 20 fused results. Offline analysis shows many relevant documents sit at fused ranks 25 to 60. Which change addresses this most directly?
options: Increase rerank depth N (and possibly each retriever's window) if latency allows
Switch the cross-encoder to a larger model
Lower RRF's k to 1
Remove the BM25 retriever
explain: A better reranker cannot score documents it never sees. Raising N (and the per-retriever windows feeding fusion) brings them into reach; the cost is one more cross-encoder pass per added candidate.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Worked toy: how averaging fake answers changes the ranking
question: In the simple model with s = 1 and b = 0.3, going from N = 8 to N = 16 samples moves the cosine from about 0.91 to about 0.93. What does this suggest?
options: Always use N = 16
Shared bias is the main error, so prompt changes cannot help
Most of the remaining gap is the shared bias, so doubling generation cost buys little
Averaging hurts beyond N = 8
explain: The ceiling is 1 over the square root of 1.09, about 0.96. Past N = 8 the independent noise is already small, so extra samples cost tokens for a small gain. Reducing the shared bias (a clearer instruction, keeping the query in the average) is the better lever.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Rejecting bad matches, warping, and direct ECC alignment
question: A drone photographs a city block twice from slightly different positions. Buildings of different heights stand on flat ground. After a RANSAC homography fit, rooftops still show strong differences while the street aligns perfectly. What is the most likely cause?
options: The RANSAC threshold was too low
Rooftops changed brightness
The homography needs more than 8 parameters, so ECC is required
Parallax: the camera center moved, so points off the ground plane do not follow the plane's homography
explain: A homography is exact only for a single plane or for pure rotation. The fitted H follows the dominant plane (the ground), and taller structures shift differently when the camera translates. ECC with MOTION_HOMOGRAPHY has the same 8-parameter limit. Remedies are a dense 3D or optical flow model, or masking out the off-plane regions.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Why epoll plus read still costs a syscall per I/O
question: Why could a server not just add its data files to epoll to get asynchronous buffered file reads?
options: epoll only supports up to 1024 descriptors
epoll works for files but only with O_DIRECT
epoll reports files as ready but read() on them returns EAGAIN
Regular files are not pollable: epoll_ctl rejects them, and a file read can block on the disk however ready the descriptor looks
explain: Readiness has no meaning for a regular file, and `epoll_ctl` returns `EPERM` for one. A read that misses the page cache must wait for the device, so the only pre-io_uring options were a thread pool or Linux AIO with its `O_DIRECT` restriction.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: One skeleton, three allocators: size classes and caches
question: Why can a size-class allocator answer free(p) without a header word in front of each object?
options: The C standard requires callers to pass the size to free
All objects in one page or span share a size class, so the allocator finds the page's metadata from the address and reads the class there
The allocator scans its free lists until it finds the neighbour of p
Each object stores its size in its last 8 bytes
explain: Segregating by size means size is a property of the container. jemalloc looks up the extent for the address, tcmalloc consults its pagemap radix tree, and mimalloc computes the page from the address. C's free does not take a size (C++ sized delete can pass one as an optimization).

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Why a healthy cluster hides consistency bugs
question: Why does Jepsen insist on talking to the database only through its client API instead of reading each replica's internal state?
options: The promise being tested is about what clients observe, so a violation in the client-visible history is exactly a broken promise
Internal state is too large to copy over SSH quickly
Opaque-box tests run faster because no instrumentation is needed
Most databases encrypt their on-disk state
explain: Consistency models are defined over the operations clients perform and the results they get back. If the client-visible history is impossible under the claimed model, the system broke its promise, whatever the internals look like. Speed and encryption are not the reason.

courseTitle: Jepsen-style fault testing: nemeses, histories and checkers
lessonTitle: Elle: catching isolation anomalies in transactions
question: Why does Elle prefer append-only lists over read-write registers?
options: Lists are cheaper to store than integers
A read of a list reveals the whole sequence of prior versions, so the version order (and ww and rw edges) can be inferred from client observations alone
Registers cannot be read inside transactions
Lists make every transaction commit, so there are no aborts to analyze
explain: A blind register write destroys history: you cannot tell which of two writes came first. A list read like [1, 2, 3] traces every version in order, and unique values recover who wrote each one.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: Search strategies and the trial budget
question: Why does OpenTuner run an ensemble of search techniques instead of picking the best one?
options: Because running techniques in parallel reduces measurement noise
Because a technique that is optimal for one kind of configuration landscape can fail on another, so credit is assigned at runtime
Because each technique explores a different part of the space by construction
Because ensembles guarantee the global optimum is found
explain: The paper's argument is that landscapes vary: a hill climber suits a smooth, monotonic space, while a discontinuous one may need evolutionary search. The AUC Bandit meta technique allocates more tests to whichever technique is currently producing new global bests. Nothing about this reduces noise or guarantees optimality.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Scaling across cores: one queue per core, rings and mempools
question: To balance load, a developer lets two threads submit I/O to the same SPDK NVMe queue pair. What happens?
options: SPDK detects it and adds a lock automatically
It works, but throughput halves
The second thread's submissions are rejected with an error
Undefined behavior: queue pairs have no locks or atomics, and SPDK does not enforce single-thread use
explain: SPDK's NVMe docs state that violating the one-thread-per-queue-pair rule is undefined behavior and is not checked, because checking would itself need a lock. Give each thread its own queue pair instead.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Vertical and horizontal fusion
question: Which pair is a horizontal fusion opportunity?
options: GELU applied to the output of a bias add
Updating 300 parameter tensors with the same Adam formula in one launch
A softmax whose output feeds a matmul
A dropout applied after GELU
explain: The 300 parameter updates are independent of one another and run the same code, so batching them into one launch is horizontal. The other three are producer-consumer pairs, which is vertical fusion.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Why a teacher's soft targets beat one-hot labels
question: A colleague says distillation is pointless if the student has the same architecture as one member of the ensemble teacher, because that architecture was already trained on the data. Based on the speech result, what is the best reply?
options: They are right: the distilled model can never beat a normally trained model of the same size
Only the ensemble matters, so the student should be deleted
The distilled single model recovered most of the ensemble's improvement, so the same architecture trained on soft targets beats the same architecture trained on labels
Distillation only helps when the student is larger than the teacher
explain: Table 1 of Hinton et al.: same architecture, same data, but trained on ensemble soft targets it reached 60.8% frame accuracy versus 58.9% with hard labels. The training targets, not just the architecture, determine what the network learns.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: When distillation works, when it fails, and what it costs
question: A born-again network (same architecture as its teacher, trained on the teacher's soft targets plus labels) beats its teacher on CIFAR-100. What does this show?
options: The student copied the teacher's weights exactly
Teachers should always be smaller than students
Distillation's benefit is not only compression: soft targets also improve generalization
Distillation only works when fidelity is perfect
explain: No compression happened, yet the student generalized better. Combined with Stanton et al.'s finding that students often do not match their teachers closely, this shows the soft-target signal acts as a regularizer, not just as a copy mechanism.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Beyond rounding: pre-RoPE keys, outliers, and FP8 in production
question: Why does KVQuant quantize keys before applying RoPE?
options: RoPE rotates channel pairs by position-dependent angles, so a steady outlier channel becomes inconsistent across tokens
RoPE makes keys larger, which overflows FP16
RoPE is only applied to values
Post-RoPE keys cannot be cached at all
explain: Per-channel quantization relies on each channel having a consistent range across tokens. Position-dependent rotation spreads a large channel's energy into its partner, widening both ranges. The cost is reapplying RoPE after dequantization.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Why the GPU prefix cache runs out, and where KV can go
question: Which system is an example of capacity offloading rather than reuse offloading?
options: LMCache storing chunks in Redis for other engines
SGLang HiCache writing radix-tree nodes to host memory
FlexGen placing part of the attention cache in CPU memory during decoding
vLLM's OffloadingConnector copying finished prompt blocks to pinned memory
explain: FlexGen offloads weights, activations and KV of the running batch to fit a huge model on a small GPU and maximize throughput. The other three save KV so later requests that share the prefix can skip prefill.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: Why wall clocks cannot order events across machines
question: In the three-node run, which pair of events is related by happened-before?
options: a3 and c2, because a3 is on A, which started the chain
c1 and c2, because they are on the same node and c1 comes first
a3 and b2, because both happen late in the run
c1 and a2, because c1 is drawn to the left of a2
explain: c1 and c2 are on the same process with c1 first, so rule 1 gives c1 happened before c2. There is no message path from a3 to anything, so a3 is concurrent with b2 and c2. c1 and a2 are concurrent too: being drawn further left is not causality.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: HLC in production: 64 bits, bounded c, and uncertainty
question: An operator lowers CockroachDB's max offset to 250 ms. Using the 80% rule, at what offset from at least half of the other nodes will a node shut itself down?
options: 250 ms
125 ms
200 ms
400 ms
explain: 0.8 x 250 = 200 ms. 400 ms is the threshold for the 500 ms default. A smaller max offset shrinks uncertainty windows (fewer restarts) but makes spurious self-termination more likely when clocks or networks wobble.

courseTitle: Late interaction: ColBERT, PLAID and ColPali
lessonTitle: Storage: why token vectors are heavy and how ColBERTv2 shrinks them
question: A 200-token passage is stored with ColBERTv2 at 2 bits per dimension, 128 dimensions. How many bytes does it take, ignoring the inverted list?
options: 7,200 bytes
6,400 bytes
51,200 bytes
800 bytes
explain: Each vector is a 4-byte centroid id plus 128 x 2 bits = 32 bytes of residual, 36 bytes total. 200 x 36 = 7,200. 6,400 forgets the centroid id, 51,200 is float16 (200 x 128 x 2), and 800 counts only the ids.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: The continuous thought: hidden state in, hidden state out
question: In latent mode at position t (between <bot> and <eot>), what is the input vector?
options: The embedding of the argmax token of softmax(W h at t-1)
A learned <pause> embedding that is the same at every latent position
The last hidden state h at position t-1, after the final normalization
The average of all previous token embeddings
explain: Coconut feeds h(t-1) directly. Taking the argmax token would be ordinary greedy CoT, and a fixed learned embedding is what pause tokens do. Only the direct feedback lets each latent input depend on the full previous computation.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: An index is a model: predicting where a key sits
question: A B-tree with pages of 128 keys and a model with min_err = -40, max_err = +60 both index the same array. In terms of the final search, which statement is right?
options: The model is worse because its errors can be negative
Both leave a range of about 100 to 128 slots to search; they are the same kind of object
The B-tree is exact and the model is approximate, so only the model needs a final search
The model needs no final search if its average error is small
explain: A page is a position estimate with min error 0 and max error 127. The model's range is 101 slots. Both end with a bounded search. That equivalence is the core observation of the paper: a B-tree already is a model with error bounds.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: Inserts, disks and when a learned index pays off
question: In Bigtable's design a weak model makes some blocks much larger than the target size tau. What breaks?
options: Lookups return wrong rows
Range scans stop working because the model is not monotonic
Nothing is incorrect; block sizes just become uneven, which can cost some read efficiency
Every lookup must now search neighbouring blocks
explain: Records are assigned to block floor(f(k) / tau) by the model itself, so the predicted block is correct by construction. A monotonic f keeps keys sorted so scans still work. A poor fit only makes block sizes less uniform.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: Training: ranking loss plus the FLOPS regularizer
question: After raising lambda_q a lot, MS MARCO MRR@10 drops slightly but queries are much faster. What most likely changed?
options: Document vectors got denser
The vocabulary shrank
The ranking loss switched to L1
Query vectors have fewer non-zeros, so fewer posting lists are traversed
explain: lambda_q only penalizes the query representation. Fewer query terms means fewer posting lists to read, at some cost in matching power.

courseTitle: Learning to rank: from RankNet to LambdaMART
lessonTitle: LambdaRank: weight each pair by what a swap does to NDCG
question: After computing lambdas for a query, a teammate finds the per-document pushes sum to 0.37. What does that tell you?
options: Nothing: sums vary from query to query
The query has more relevant than irrelevant documents
The learning rate is too high
There is a bug: each pair adds equal and opposite pushes, so the total must be 0
explain: Every pair contributes +lambda to one document and -lambda to the other, so the sum over a query is exactly zero (up to rounding).

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: The state is a key-value memory, and it fills up
question: In the toy, why did $k_A$ and $k_B$ read back perfectly after the first two writes?
options: Because they were written first
Because the values 4 and 2 are small
Because the keys are unit length and orthogonal, so $k_A^\top k_B = 0$ and nothing leaks
Because S was reset between writes
explain: Reading $Sk_A = 4(k_A^\top k_A) + 2(k_B^\top k_A) = 4\cdot 1 + 2\cdot 0 = 4$. Orthonormal keys make the memory exact; overlap is what causes interference.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Why relevance labels are the bottleneck of search evaluation
question: Bing selects its judge prompt by agreement with which reference?
options: Labels from typical crowd workers
The judge's own labels from a previous week
Careful feedback from real searchers who had the information need
Click-through rate on the live search page
explain: Thomas et al. use first-party gold labels from searchers who had the need, because third-party labellers (crowd or staff) can systematically misread intent. Agreement with crowd labels would only reproduce the crowd's mistakes.

courseTitle: LLM-as-judge for relevance labeling
lessonTitle: Circularity, gaming, and running an LLM judge safely
question: Your team's reranker is a fine-tuned copy of the same LLM and prompt used to label your offline test set. Offline NDCG@10 jumps from 0.71 to 0.93. What is the most defensible next step?
options: Ship it: a 0.22 gain is far outside noise
Re-evaluate with labels from humans or a judge independent of the reranker, at least on a sample and on the top competing systems
Report the gain with quadratic-weighted kappa instead
Raise the judge temperature to reduce bias
explain: This is the circular setup Faggioli et al. warned about and Clarke and Dietz demonstrated: scores near the ceiling under the judge's own labels while human-labelled NDCG barely moves. Only an independent reference can tell whether the gain is real.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: Fragmentation, and block tables as page tables
question: In the contiguous simulation, 12.8% of the pool was free yet the next request in line could not start. Which kind of waste is this?
options: Internal fragmentation
Reserved slots
Activation memory
External fragmentation
explain: Free memory existed, but not as one contiguous run long enough for the waiting request's reservation. That is external fragmentation. With fixed-size blocks any free block is usable, so external fragmentation disappears; the 0.5% left free in the paged run is just too few blocks for the next prompt.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Few-shot examples and asking the model to reason first
question: Your sentiment prompt has four examples, all labeled positive, and the model now labels most neutral reviews positive. What is the most likely cause?
options: Four examples are too few for in-context learning
The examples are not diverse, so the model picked up 'answer positive' as part of the pattern
Examples only affect format, never labels
The model needs gradient updates to learn labels
explain: Examples teach whatever pattern they share, intended or not. Anthropic's advice is to make examples diverse and to cover edge cases. Brown et al. show that examples steer behavior with no gradient updates at all.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Validation, retries and the pitfalls of strict formats
question: A summarization job uses a strict schema with max_tokens set to 200. About 3 percent of replies fail to parse even though constrained decoding is on. What is the most likely cause?
options: The decoder's mask has a bug that lets invalid tokens through
Those replies hit the 200-token limit and were cut off mid-JSON
The model refused, which always produces invalid JSON
JSON Schema cannot describe summaries
explain: A mask keeps every prefix valid and allows stopping only at an accept state, but the token limit cuts generation off regardless. Check the stop reason (max_tokens or incomplete) and raise the limit or shorten the output.

courseTitle: LLM query parsing: natural language to structured filters
lessonTitle: Latency budgets, caching and parallel fallback
question: Which cache key is safest for storing parsed filter objects?
options: The raw query string exactly as typed
The normalized query string alone
The normalized query plus the user's session ID
The normalized query plus the schema version and vocabulary version
explain: Raw strings fragment the cache on case and spacing. Without versions, a schema or dictionary change keeps serving stale parses (an old field name, a city ID that was split). The session ID would make the cache nearly useless, since the parse does not depend on who asked.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Cutting decode: FIRST and single-token listwise ranking
question: At k=100, L=100, w=20, FIRST brings our modeled query latency from 10.35 s to 2.39 s. Which next change cuts FIRST's latency the most?
options: Raising the window step s while keeping w = 20, which removes windows and their prefill
Asking for a shorter permutation format
Using a higher sampling temperature
Adding a reasoning step before the ranking
explain: FIRST has no permutation to shorten, so the remaining time is prefill on a chain of windows. Fewer windows (or fewer tokens per window) is what is left. A reasoning step would add decode tokens back.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Pointwise: yes/no relevance and query likelihood
question: Your API returns only generated text, no log-probabilities. Which pointwise method can you still run, and with what limitation?
options: Query likelihood, because it uses teacher forcing
Neither; pointwise prompts cannot work without fine-tuning
Yes/No generation, but you only get a binary label, so many passages tie and the ranking is coarse
Both, as long as you set temperature to 0
explain: Query likelihood needs the probability of the given query tokens, which a text-only API cannot provide. Yes/No still produces an answer, but without p(Yes) you only get two buckets, so passages inside a bucket keep their original order.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Position bias, robustness and distilled rerankers
question: Your listwise reranker works well on BM25 input but degrades badly when you switch the first stage to a new retriever that returns candidates in a near-random order. Which fix targets the cause?
options: Increase the window step so fewer windows are needed
Lower the temperature to 0
Shuffle the input several times and aggregate the rankings, or use a student trained with shuffled inputs
Switch to query likelihood, which is order-free but needs no changes
explain: The symptom is order sensitivity: failures and the one-pass guarantee both lean on a good initial order. Permutation self-consistency marginalizes the order out, and RankVicuna/RankZephyr train on shuffled inputs for the same reason. Temperature 0 makes outputs repeatable, not order-invariant.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: RANSAC: keeping only matches that agree on one homography
question: Inlier ratio is 0.5 and you need 99% confidence. How many RANSAC iterations does a homography (s = 4) need?
explain: N = log(0.01)/log(1 - 0.5^4) = log(0.01)/log(0.9375) = 71.36, rounded up to 72. 16 is 1/w^4, the expected number of draws to see the first clean sample, which is not enough for 99% confidence. 567 is the answer for w = 0.3.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: The Michael-Scott queue: a dummy node and helping
question: A thread in enqueue reads Tail = X and finds X.next is not NULL. What does the algorithm do?
options: Wait until the thread that linked X.next swings Tail
Try to CAS Tail forward to X.next, then retry its own enqueue
Link its node after X anyway
Return failure because the queue is full
explain: That is E13: Tail is lagging, so the thread helps advance it and loops. Waiting would make the algorithm blocking, and linking after X would break the list because X is not the last node.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Why one regular expression per format does not scale
question: Why is "88 percent of Thunderbird's templates are missing from a 2,000-line sample" a problem for a hand-written regex set, but not fatal for a template miner?
options: The miner has already seen all 1,241 templates during training
The miner stores raw lines, so it can re-derive templates on demand
The miner creates a new template group the first time it sees an unmatched line, so unseen formats cost nothing extra
Rare templates are noise and a miner correctly discards them
explain: An online miner's whole job is to open a new group for a line that matches nothing. A regex set has to be edited by a person before the new format parses at all, and until then those lines fall into an unparsed bucket. Rare templates are usually the valuable ones: error-level messages are rare by construction.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Drift when a release changes the format, and a pipeline that holds
question: Your log volume quadruples and the parser falls behind. Which of the Huawei deployment's four measures gives both a throughput win and an accuracy win?
options: Partitioning by verbosity level and component, since different levels and components come from different logging statements: fewer candidates per partition, and the partitions parse in parallel
Raising the similarity threshold so fewer comparisons are needed
Reducing the tree depth to shorten every walk
Sampling one line in four and extrapolating the counts
explain: Partitioning narrows the search space, which speeds parsing, and it also removes the chance of merging templates across components, which helps accuracy. It is also the parallelization key they used with Spark. Threshold and depth are accuracy trade-offs, not free wins, and sampling destroys exactly the rare error templates you most want to count.

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: Hiding communication, causal balance and Ulysses
question: You move a Ring Attention job from NVLink (300 GB/s) to a 25 GB/s network with the same GPUs (312 TFLOP/s). Roughly what minimum block size now hides communication?
options: 1,040 tokens, unchanged since hidden size cancels
About 87 tokens
About 12,480 tokens
It can never be hidden on a slower link
explain: c >= F / B = 312e12 / 25e9 = 12,480. Bandwidth dropped 12x, so the minimum block grows 12x. The hidden size cancels, but the bandwidth does not.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Recurrent depth at scale: prelude, core block and coda
question: A colleague simplifies the design: set s0 = e and stop feeding e into later iterations. What does the paper's reasoning predict?
options: Nothing changes, because e is already inside s0
The loop becomes less stable: its end point depends on the starting point, not on continued use of the input
Training becomes cheaper and generalizes better because the adapter is removed
The model becomes a Universal Transformer and gains Turing completeness
explain: The authors argue the input must be injected at every step, as data enters every step of gradient descent. With e only in the initial state, the iteration cannot behave like a stable, input-dependent operator; its result depends on the boundary condition.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Approximate unlearning: gradient ascent, collapse and NPO
question: During NPO with beta = 1, a forget example's probability is now 1% of the reference model's. Compared with plain gradient ascent, how strongly does this example still push the weights?
options: Equally strongly, NPO only changes the loss value, not the gradient
About 2% as strongly, the weight is 2(0.01)/(0.01 + 1) = 0.020
About 50% as strongly, the weight bottoms out at 0.5
Twice as strongly, because NPO doubles the gradient
explain: NPO's gradient is the GA gradient times W = 2r^b / (r^b + 1). With r = 0.01 and b = 1 that is 0.02 / 1.01, about 0.020. The weight stays near 1 only for very small beta, where NPO behaves like GA; there is no floor at 0.5, it keeps falling toward 0.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Truncate, then re-normalize: the mechanics on a toy vector
question: You truncate stored 1024-d unit vectors to 256 dims and forget to re-normalize them. Queries are truncated and re-normalized. You rank by dot product. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: re-normalizing the query is enough to restore cosine order
All scores shrink by the same factor, so the order is unchanged
Scores now mix angle with each document's prefix length, so documents with long prefixes are favored
Dot products become negative for every document
explain: Each stored prefix keeps a different share of its length (0.903 for X and 0.515 for Y in the toy). The dot product multiplies cosine by that length, so long-prefix documents get a boost unrelated to relevance. Normalizing only the query scales every score equally and cannot fix it.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, SP, CP and MFU
lessonTitle: Tensor parallelism: column and row splits of the MLP and attention
question: For a fixed model, a team doubles TP from 4 to 8 inside a server. Per GPU and per layer, how does TP communication volume change?
options: It halves, because each GPU holds half as many weights
It stays the same
It grows from 6 bsh to 7 bsh, about 17% more
It doubles
explain: Volume is 8bsh(t-1)/t: 8 x 3/4 = 6 bsh at t = 4 and 8 x 7/8 = 7 bsh at t = 8. Communication does not shrink with more TP ranks while compute per GPU halves, so the communication share of each step rises.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Free memory you cannot use: two kinds of fragmentation
question: A heap has 6 KiB free in six 1 KiB holes and gets a 2 KiB request. Which change would let the request succeed without growing the heap?
options: Rounding the request up to 4 KiB
Switching to a faster free-list search
Freeing one more object that sits between two holes, so they coalesce
Adding a second free list for 1 KiB holes
explain: The request fails because no two free bytes are adjacent. Freeing an object between two holes lets the allocator coalesce them into a 3 KiB hole. Search speed and extra lists do not create contiguity, and rounding up makes the request harder to fit.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: Why two threads can disagree about what happened first
question: On an x86 machine the SB test (x = 1; r1 = y in one thread, y = 1; r2 = x in the other) sometimes ends with r1 = 0 and r2 = 0. What is the best explanation?
options: The cache coherence protocol lost one of the writes
Each core's store sat in its store buffer while the same core's later load read the old value from memory
The two threads ran on the same core, so they could not see each other
x86 reorders every pair of memory operations freely
explain: Both writes eventually reach memory, so nothing was lost. x86-TSO only allows a store to be delayed past a later load, which is exactly what the store buffer does. Threads time-sliced on one hardware thread share one store buffer, so they would not produce it (two hyperthreads of one core have separate buffers and can), and x86 does not reorder loads with loads or stores with stores.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: From orderings to instructions: x86-64, ARM64, and choosing
question: Code using `Relaxed` for a ready flag passes millions of test runs on x86-64 CI but corrupts data on an ARM64 server. What is the most accurate diagnosis?
options: ARM64 has a broken cache coherence protocol
The code was always wrong: x86-64 gives acquire/release ordering to plain loads and stores, which hid the missing Release/Acquire
x86-64 runs Relaxed operations as SeqCst, so the code is correct on x86-64 and only ARM64 needs a fix
The ARM64 compiler has a bug
explain: The memory model never promised ordering for Relaxed. x86-TSO happens to prevent the message-passing reordering, but the compiler could still reorder the operations even there. The fix is a Release store and an Acquire load, which costs nothing extra on x86-64.

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Epoch-based reclamation: free garbage two epochs later
question: A request handler calls `epoch::pin()`, reads a node from a lock-free map, then makes a 2-second network call before dropping the guard. What is the main problem?
options: The node may be freed during the network call
The network call will deadlock
No memory retired by any thread during those 2 seconds can be reclaimed
The guard will be dropped automatically after 128 pins
explain: The node is safe; the guard guarantees that. The cost lands on everyone else: the pinned thread keeps the global epoch from advancing past its epoch plus one, so all garbage retired meanwhile waits. Copy what you need, drop the guard, then do the slow call.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Triplet loss: the margin and easy, semi-hard, hard negatives
question: Anchor-positive distance is 0.40 and margin is 0.2. A negative sits at 0.50. Which band is it in and what is the loss?
options: Semi-hard, loss 0.10
Easy, loss 0
Hard, loss 0.30
Semi-hard, loss 0.30
explain: 0.40 < 0.50 < 0.60, so the negative is further than the positive but inside the margin: semi-hard. Loss = 0.40 - 0.50 + 0.2 = 0.10.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: When the optimizer deletes the code you meant to time
question: Which change alone stops clang from folding `bench_fold` into one multiply?
options: Returning s from the function
Marking compute as inline
Passing the input as a function parameter whose value the compiler cannot see, instead of the literal 42
Increasing n to 10 billion
explain: bench_fold already returns s, and that did not help: folding needs only that the input be known. An inline hint changes nothing (compute was already inlined). A larger n changes the multiply, not the strategy. An unknown input stops the folding, but clang still runs compute once before the loop and multiplies by n (hoisting, next lesson).

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Miles in one picture: slime's loop built for frontier scale
question: You need to post-train a 700B-parameter MoE whose training job spans several racks and needs expert parallelism. Which training backend do the Miles docs point you to?
options: Megatron-LM, the default and the backend for 100B+ MoE models that need model parallelism
FSDP, because it loads the Hugging Face checkpoint with no conversion
torchtitan, because it is driven as a black box
Any of them; the backend only changes checkpoint format
explain: The training-backend page says to use Megatron-LM for large models and anything that needs real parallelism, such as a 100B+ MoE or a job spanning racks. FSDP is the fast path for new architectures and models that fit under data parallelism alone. The backend changes how the model is split, not only its checkpoints.

courseTitle: Miles: production RL post-training forked from slime
lessonTitle: Moving a trillion parameters, and surviving dead engines
question: A disk-delta update in XOR encoding is accidentally applied twice to the same rollout host. What state does the host end up in?
options: The new weights, because XOR is idempotent
The previous weights, because XOR applied twice cancels itself
A corrupted mix, detected only at the next step
The base checkpoint from step 0
explain: XOR is an involution: (w XOR d) XOR d = w. So a second application silently undoes the update. That is why the report says an XOR delta must be applied exactly once and against its declared base, and why the overwrite encoding exists for retry-prone setups.

courseTitle: ML for systems: learned indexes, caching and scheduling
lessonTitle: Decima: learning a cluster scheduler with reinforcement learning
question: Why does Decima end training episodes at a random, memoryless time instead of a fixed horizon?
options: Random cutoffs make the simulator faster
With a fixed horizon, the agent can learn to postpone large jobs until just before the episode ends, a strategy that fails in a real cluster that never stops
REINFORCE requires episodes of random length to converge
Fixed horizons cause the graph neural network to overflow
explain: If the end is predictable, delaying large jobs past it hides their cost from the reward. A memoryless cutoff gives no time at which deferring work becomes free, so the agent has to schedule as if the cluster runs forever.

courseTitle: Multi-head latent attention (MLA)
lessonTitle: Absorbing the up-projections: attend in latent space
question: In the toy, the absorbed query for head 2 is (1.5, 0.5). What is head 2's raw score against token 3, whose latent is $c_3 = (1, 0.5)$?
explain: $1.5 \times 1 + 0.5 \times 0.5 = 1.75$, the same as $q \cdot k_3$ with the rebuilt key $k_3 = (1.5, 0.5)$: $1 \times 1.5 + 0.5 \times 0.5 = 1.75$.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: The multi-query pipeline: generate, retrieve in parallel, merge
question: You configure LlamaIndex `QueryFusionRetriever(num_queries=4, ...)` with one retriever. How many LLM-generated queries and how many searches does one call make?
options: 4 generated, 4 searches
4 generated, 5 searches
3 generated, 4 searches
1 generated, 4 searches
explain: num_queries counts the original. The prompt asks the LLM for num_queries - 1 = 3 queries, and the original plus those 3 are each searched once per retriever: 4 searches. Setting num_queries=1 disables generation.

courseTitle: Multi-query retrieval: many phrasings, one fused result
lessonTitle: Drift, redundancy, reranker budgets, and when to skip it
question: The LLM sometimes returns phrasings that shift the question to a neighboring topic. Which change most directly limits the damage?
options: Raise N so the drifted phrasing is outvoted
Keep the original query in the set and inspect or filter generated queries that look off-topic
Replace RRF with an unranked union
Drop the original query to avoid bias
explain: The original query cannot drift and anchors fusion. Filtering clearly off-topic rewrites (or constraining the prompt) removes the junk list. Raising N adds cost and may add more drift; a union passes drifted results straight through.

courseTitle: Multi-stage retrieval: designing the retrieve-then-rerank cascade
lessonTitle: LLM listwise reranking and distilling it into cheaper stages
question: RankGPT reranks M = 100 passages with w = 20 and s = 10. You switch to w = 20, s = 5 to give passages more chances to move. How many LLM calls does one pass now make?
explain: ceil((100 - 20) / 5) + 1 = 16 + 1 = 17 calls, reading 17 x 20 = 340 passages. Smaller steps mean more overlap and almost double the cost of s = 10. The guaranteed-correct top also grows, from w - s = 10 to 15.

courseTitle: Multi-token prediction: training GPTs to look ahead
lessonTitle: DeepSeek-V3: sequential MTP modules with a full causal chain
question: At depth k = 2 in DeepSeek-V3's scheme, which inputs does the module use for position i, and which token does it predict?
options: h_i from the main model and Emb(t_i+1); predicts t_i+2
h_i from depth 1 and Emb(t_i+2); predicts t_i+3
h_i from depth 1 and Emb(t_i+3); predicts t_i+3
Only Emb(t_i+2); predicts t_i+3
explain: Depth k combines h at depth k - 1 with the embedding of t(i+k) and predicts t(i+k+1). For k = 2 that is h from depth 1, Emb(t(i+2)), and target t(i+3).

courseTitle: Muon, Shampoo and SOAP: optimizers that treat weights as matrices
lessonTitle: Muon: orthogonalize the momentum with a few matrix multiplies
question: A colleague raises Muon's Newton-Schulz steps from 5 to 10 to get a more exactly orthogonal update. Based on the Moonlight report, what should they expect?
options: Noticeably lower loss, since the update is now exactly UV^T
Divergence, because the tuned polynomial is unstable after 5 steps
A more accurate orthogonalization but no better model, at twice the Newton-Schulz cost
No change at all in the update, because the iteration converged after 5 steps
explain: Moonlight reports that $N = 10$ gives a more accurate orthogonalization than $N = 5$ but does not improve performance, so they kept 5. With the tuned coefficients the values keep bouncing within roughly $[0.7, 1.2]$, so the update does change, just not in a way that helps.

courseTitle: muP: tune a small model, transfer hyperparameters to a large one
lessonTitle: What breaks in SP after a single training step
question: You train a hidden d x d layer with Adam. You widen d from 1024 to 4096 and want the per-coordinate change of $\Delta W\,x$ after one step to stay the same. What should the layer's learning rate do?
options: Stay the same, because Adam already normalizes gradients
Be divided by 4, the width ratio
Be divided by 2, the square root of the width ratio
Be multiplied by 4
explain: Adam makes each entry of $\Delta W$ about $\pm\eta$ regardless of width, and $\Delta W$ is aligned with $x$, so $\Delta W\,x$ entries scale like $\eta \cdot \text{fan\_in}$. Keeping them fixed when fan_in grows 4x means dividing $\eta$ by 4. The square-root rule would be right for random, uncorrelated matrices, not for updates.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: From a racy flag to a correct spin lock
question: A colleague writes unlock as `locked.store(false, Relaxed)` to save a few cycles. Lock still uses `swap(true, Acquire)`. What can go wrong?
options: The next owner may not see writes made inside the previous critical section
Two threads can own the lock at once
Nothing: Acquire on the lock side is enough
The lock can never be acquired again
explain: Mutual exclusion still holds, because the swap is atomic regardless of ordering. What breaks is visibility: without a Release store there is no happens-before edge from the old owner's writes to the new owner's reads, so the new owner may read stale data.

courseTitle: Mutexes, spinlocks and futexes: how locks really wait
lessonTitle: Locks in real systems: kernels, priorities and choices
question: Kernel code running in an interrupt handler needs to protect a counter shared with a normal kernel thread. Which lock fits?
options: struct mutex, because it spins optimistically first
A futex
A spin lock taken with interrupts disabled (for example spin_lock_irqsave) on the thread side
No lock: interrupts cannot run concurrently with threads
explain: Interrupt handlers cannot sleep, so sleeping locks like mutex are out. The thread side must also disable interrupts while holding the spin lock, or the interrupt could fire on the same CPU and spin forever on a lock its own CPU holds.

courseTitle: MVCC and transaction isolation levels
lessonTitle: Serializable Snapshot Isolation: catching dangerous structures
question: Two Serializable transactions each run SELECT ... FROM accounts WHERE id = <own id> on a table with no index on id, then UPDATE their own, different row. PostgreSQL aborts one even though no serial order would differ. Why?
options: SSI blocked on an SIRead lock and the lock timed out
A deadlock between the two updates
Read Committed was used by mistake
A false positive: each sequential scan took a relation-level SIRead lock, so each update formed an rw edge with the other's read
explain: SIRead locks never block, so there is no timeout or deadlock. Without an index the SELECT uses a sequential scan, which locks the whole relation, so the other transaction's update of a different row still looks like an rw conflict. Edges both ways form a dangerous structure even though neither read cared about the other row. An index on id would avoid it.

courseTitle: Named entity recognition: tagging spans in text
lessonTitle: The metric: entity-level micro F1 with exact span match
question: A tagger predicts `B-PER I-PER` over the three tokens `Mary Jane Smith` where gold is one PER spanning all three. What does this contribute to the entity-level counts?
options: 1 TP, since two of three tokens are inside the right entity
1 TP and 1 FP, for getting the type right but the end wrong
0.67 TP under partial credit
1 FP and 1 FN, because the predicted span is not in the gold set and the gold span was not predicted
explain: Exact match has no partial credit. PER(0,1) is not PER(0,2), so the prediction is a false positive and the gold entity is a false negative. One wrong boundary tag costs two errors, which is why boundary quality drives entity F1 much harder than token accuracy suggests.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: Why long context needs sparsity, and why bolt-on sparsity disappoints
question: A model uses GQA with 8 query heads per KV group. A sparse method lets each head choose 4 of 64 KV blocks independently, and the heads mostly disagree. During decoding, roughly what happens to memory traffic per group?
options: It drops to 4/64 of dense, since each head reads 4 blocks
It drops to somewhere up to 32/64 of dense, because the union of the heads' picks must be loaded
It is unchanged, because sparse methods never reduce memory reads
It increases, because sparse methods must read all keys to score them
explain: Heads in a GQA group share one KV cache, so the kernel loads the union of their selections: up to 8 x 4 = 32 distinct blocks. Compute per head is 4/64, but decoding is memory bound, so the union is what sets latency. This is exactly why NSA forces one shared selection per group.

courseTitle: Native sparse attention: NSA and DeepSeek Sparse Attention
lessonTitle: DeepSeek Sparse Attention: a lightning indexer picks tokens
question: During DSA's dense warm-up, what is the indexer trained to predict?
options: The next token, using the language modeling loss
Which tokens NSA's compression branch would select
The main attention distribution for each query, summed over heads and L1-normalized, via a KL loss
A binary label for whether each token is in the top 2048
explain: The target $p_{t,:}$ is the dense main attention summed over heads and normalized. The indexer's softmax is pulled toward it with KL divergence while the main model is frozen, so the indexer learns which tokens the model actually attends to before sparsity is switched on.

courseTitle: Near-duplicate image search with perceptual hashes
lessonTitle: Searching millions of hashes: BK-trees and multi-index hashing
question: In a BK-tree search with radius 2, the current node is at distance 6 from the query. Which children are visited?
options: Children on edges 4 to 8
Only children on edges 0 to 2
All children, because the node did not match
None, because the node did not match
explain: A child on edge e is at distance e from this node, so by the triangle inequality its distance to the query is at least |6 - e|. That is at most 2 only when e is between 4 and 8. Not matching the node itself does not stop the descent.

courseTitle: NeMo RL: NVIDIA's Ray-based post-training library
lessonTitle: Training backends (Automodel, Megatron) and generation backends
question: You want to post-train a model with hundreds of billions of parameters and 16k-token sequences. Which choice matches what the docs recommend?
options: Megatron backend, configured under policy.megatron_cfg, with its optimizer under megatron_cfg.optimizer
Automodel backend with vLLM, since it is the default
Hugging Face generation backend for rollouts
Convert to a Megatron checkpoint by hand and point NeMo RL at it
explain: The training-backends doc positions Megatron for scaling to very large models, and the README lists larger models with longer sequences under Megatron Core parallelisms. NeMo RL takes only HF checkpoints as input and converts them itself, so a hand-made Megatron checkpoint is not the documented path.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: First touch: the thread that writes a page first picks its node
question: A server allocates a large buffer pool at startup and fills it from a single loader thread. Benchmarks show workers on node 1 are slower than workers on node 0. Which change fixes placement with the least code?
options: Call malloc from each worker thread instead of the loader
Add a read-only warm-up pass on each worker after loading
Increase the size of the pool so it spans both nodes
Have each pinned worker write its own share of the pool during startup
explain: Placement happens on the first write, not on malloc and not on a read (a first read of anonymous memory maps the shared zero page). Having each pinned worker write its share first puts those pages on the worker's node.

courseTitle: NUMA: placing memory and threads on multi-socket machines
lessonTitle: Keeping threads near their data: pinning, balancing and diagnosis
question: numastat shows numa_miss = 0 and numa_foreign = 0 on every node, yet threads on node 1 see slow memory. Which explanation fits?
options: Allocations were local to the allocating thread, but the pages are used by threads on another node
The counters are broken on this kernel
Node 1 has no memory, so its CPUs never miss
explain: numastat counts where allocations were satisfied relative to the allocator's preference. A single initializer thread produces perfect counters while the consumers on node 1 read remotely. Check /proc/PID/numa_maps for page locations.

courseTitle: NVMe and SSD internals: FTL, garbage collection, write amplification
lessonTitle: Wear leveling, TRIM, hot and cold data, endurance
question: A database deletes old SSTable files but the file system is mounted without discard and fstrim never runs. What happens inside the SSD?
options: Nothing changes: deleted files free their flash pages automatically
The FTL still considers those LBAs live, so cleaning keeps copying dead data and write amplification rises
The drive becomes read-only
The data is erased immediately to free space
explain: Deleting a file only updates file system metadata. Until the LBAs are trimmed (deallocated), the drive must preserve their contents and copies them during every cleaning of their blocks.

courseTitle: Object detection and counting
lessonTitle: Scoring a detector: precision, recall, AP and COCO mAP
question: Two detectors have the same AP at IoU 0.5, but detector X has much higher AP@[.5:.95]. What does that tell you?
options: X finds more objects
X is faster
X has fewer classes
X's boxes are more tightly aligned with the ground truth
explain: At IoU 0.5 both find and rank objects equally well. The stricter thresholds (up to 0.95) only reward detections whose boxes overlap the truth very closely, so X's advantage is localization precision.

courseTitle: Object storage-backed databases: S3-native and tiered storage
lessonTitle: Committing to object storage: metadata, CAS and fencing
question: New writer B (epoch 2) tries its fencing write at WAL slot 2 and gets 412. Reading slot 2, it finds an SST from old writer A with epoch 1. What should B do?
options: Halt, because it lost the race
Overwrite slot 2 without a condition, since its epoch is higher
Retry the fencing write at slot 3
Wait for A's lease to expire, then retry slot 2
explain: This is RFC-0001's second example. A simply got one more SST in before B's fence. Because the winner's epoch is older, B moves to the next ID and retries; once its fence lands, A will hit B's SST and halt. Halting is only right when the winner's epoch is newer. Overwriting would destroy A's acknowledged data.

courseTitle: Observability: metrics, traces, dashboards and SLOs
lessonTitle: Counters, gauges, histograms, and the quantile you must not average
question: You must report the fraction of requests served under 300 ms, and you want to be able to change that threshold later without redeploying the service. Which instrument?
options: A histogram with a boundary at 0.3, since stored bucket counts let the server compute any threshold that has a boundary
A summary configured with quantile 0.95
A gauge set to the duration of the last request
A counter incremented whenever a request finishes under 300 ms
explain: The counter answers today's question exactly but hard-codes 300 ms into the binary. The summary fixes the quantiles, not a threshold, at instrumentation time. The gauge throws away every request but the last. Only the histogram keeps counts you can query differently later, limited to the boundaries you chose.

courseTitle: OCR and document understanding: from pixels to fields
lessonTitle: Reading a line: CRNN features and CTC decoding
question: A greedy CTC decoder sees the argmax path  - - c c - a a - t t - t  (with - as blank). What does it output?
options: cat
catt
ccaatt
catat
explain: Merge repeats first: - c - a - t - t. Then drop blanks: c a t t. The blank between the two t groups keeps them as separate characters.

courseTitle: Building large projects from source (CMake, CUDA builds)
lessonTitle: CMake in three phases: configure, generate, build
question: After a first configure with GCC, you run `CXX=clang++ cmake -S . -B build`. The build still uses GCC. Why?
options: CMake only reads CXX on Windows
Ninja caches the compiler path in .ninja_log
clang++ must be passed with -G
The C++ compiler was fixed in CMakeCache.txt on the first configure and cannot be changed in that build tree
explain: CMAKE_CXX_COMPILER is chosen on the first configure of a build tree (from CXX or -D) and the docs say it cannot be changed afterwards. Use a new build directory or cmake --fresh.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: What CI does when you open a pull request
question: A job in your fork PR fails at a step that uploads benchmark results using `secrets.BENCH_TOKEN`. The same job passes on the maintainers' pushes to `main`. Why?
options: Secrets other than `GITHUB_TOKEN` are not passed to runners for workflows triggered from forks
Fork PRs run on slower runners, so the upload times out
Secrets expire after each push
The workflow file in your fork is ignored
explain: The GitHub docs state that, with the exception of `GITHUB_TOKEN`, secrets are not passed to the runner when a workflow is triggered from a forked repository, and that token is read-only there. This protects the project from PRs that try to exfiltrate secrets.

courseTitle: CI pipelines and test suites: from red checks to reliable tests
lessonTitle: Diagnosing and fixing flaky tests: order, state and timing
question: Your PR adds a feature, and an unrelated-looking test `test_download_retry` fails in CI once. Which response is best?
options: Add `@pytest.mark.flaky(reruns=5)` to the test in your PR
Push an empty commit until CI goes green
Run the node id locally on the merged branch; if it passes, check whether it also fails on `main` or other PRs and mention that evidence in the PR
Set `fail-fast: false` in the workflow
explain: Gather evidence before labelling a failure flaky: reproduce on the merged code, then look for the same failure without your change. Silencing or repeatedly re-running a test you may have broken is exactly how real regressions get merged.

courseTitle: Code review: responding to and giving review
lessonTitle: GitHub mechanics: decisions, suggestions and merge rules
question: Your PR was approved, then you pushed one more commit fixing a typo in code. The repository requires reviews and has stale review dismissal on. What happens?
options: The approval stays because the change was small
The PR merges automatically
The approval is dismissed and the PR needs a new approval before merging
GitHub reverts your commit
explain: With required reviews and stale review dismissal enabled, any code-modifying commit pushed to an approved PR dismisses the approval. GitHub does not judge whether the change was small.

courseTitle: Contribution norms: CONTRIBUTING, issues, conduct and AI policies
lessonTitle: AI-assisted contributions: label it, keep a human in the loop, or not
question: An LLVM issue is labelled `good first issue`. You can fix it in two minutes with a coding agent and you will carefully review the result. Is that allowed under LLVM's policy?
options: Yes, as long as you review the output and add Assisted-by
Yes, but only if a maintainer approves the agent first
No, because LLVM bans all AI tools
No: AI tools must not be used to fix good first issues, which exist as learning opportunities
explain: LLVM generally allows tools with a human in the loop, but makes a specific exception: AI tools must not be used for issues labelled good first issue, since automating them squanders the learning opportunity.

courseTitle: Git workflow for pull requests: fork, branch, rebase, sign-off
lessonTitle: Folding review fixes into the right commit with --fixup
question: You want to fix a typo in the *message* of an earlier commit without changing any code, and let autosquash apply it. Which command creates the right commit?
options: `git commit --fixup=<commit>`
`git commit --squash=<commit>`
`git commit --fixup=reword:<commit>`
`git commit --amend`
explain: `--fixup=reword:` creates an `amend!` commit that replaces the target's message and ignores staged changes. Plain `--fixup` keeps the target's message. `--amend` only rewrites the latest commit, not an earlier one.

courseTitle: Open source licenses, CLAs and the DCO
lessonTitle: Copyleft: when you must share source, and with whom
question: Which change to a proprietary app is most likely to pull it under GPL-3.0 terms when shipped?
options: Calling a GPL-3.0 command-line tool through a pipe
Putting a GPL-3.0 tool on the same installer as a separate program
Statically linking a GPL-3.0 library into the app's executable
Reading a file format that a GPL-3.0 program also reads
explain: Code in the same executable is one program in the FSF's view, and GPLv3 section 5(c) then covers the whole work. Pipes and aggregates keep programs separate, and a file format is not code you copied.

courseTitle: Performance PRs: benchmark evidence and regression checks
lessonTitle: What a reviewer needs before merging a speedup
question: Besides numbers that back up a claimed gain, what else does the kernel's patch guide ask for in an optimization patch?
options: A link to a third-party benchmark website
Proof that the gain holds on every architecture Linux supports
A description of the non-obvious costs and expected downsides, so the reviewer can weigh them
Nothing else: numbers alone are sufficient
explain: The guide says optimizations usually trade CPU, memory and readability, or one workload against another, and asks you to describe the expected downsides so the reviewer can weigh costs against benefits.

courseTitle: Reading a large codebase: search, trace and dig through history
lessonTitle: Search that narrows: git grep, ripgrep and word matches
question: Which GitHub code search query finds where Redis **defines** a function named lookupKeyRead?
options: `repo:redis/redis lookupKeyRead`
`symbol:lookupKeyRead`
`repo:redis/redis symbol:lookupKeyRead`
`repo:redis symbol:lookupKeyRead`
explain: symbol: matches definitions and repo: scopes to one repository. repo: needs the full owner/name, since partial repository names are not supported. A bare term matches any file whose content or path contains it, so the first query returns every call site too.

courseTitle: Reproducing bugs: minimal repros, delta debugging and git bisect
lessonTitle: Shrinking a failing program by hand
question: You remove a block of logging setup and the program no longer fails at all. What does this tell you?
options: The logging setup is part of what triggers the bug, so it must stay in the repro (perhaps in a smaller form)
The bug was in your logging code, so it is not worth reporting
Nothing; flaky programs sometimes pass, so delete the block anyway
explain: If the failure disappears when a piece is removed, that piece is needed to trigger it. Put it back and try to shrink it rather than delete it. It does not prove the bug is in your code. If you suspect flakiness, rerun several times before concluding anything (lesson 5).

courseTitle: Writing a reviewable pull request
lessonTitle: Why a reviewer sends a big pull request back
question: Which PR is most likely to be flagged as too large, according to Google's guidance?
options: A 200-line bug fix in one file
A change that only deletes three obsolete files (900 removed lines)
A 200-line change spread across 50 files
A 60-line change with 40 lines of tests
explain: Size includes spread. The guide says a 200-line change in one file might be okay, but across 50 files it would usually be too large. Deleting whole files counts as roughly one line each, and tests belong in the change.

courseTitle: PagedAttention and prefix caching
lessonTitle: Block tables: virtual memory for the KV cache
question: A kernel reads the KV of position `pos` at `base + pos * bytes_per_token`, as a contiguous kernel would. After switching to paged storage, what goes wrong?
options: It reads the right tokens only while the sequence fits in its first block; later positions land in whatever block happens to sit next in memory
Nothing, because physical blocks are allocated in increasing order
It reads correct data but more slowly
It fails only for requests that share blocks
explain: Logical blocks are mapped to arbitrary physical blocks (7, 1, 3 in the example). Only offsets inside a block are contiguous, so every access must go through the block table: `table[pos // B] * B + pos % B`.

courseTitle: perf and flame graphs
lessonTitle: From perf.data to folded stacks
question: A folded file contains `app;main;run;parse 40` and `app;main;run 10`. What are the self and total sample counts of `run`?
options: self 50, total 50
self 10, total 50
self 0, total 50
self 10, total 10
explain: run is the leaf only in the second line, so self = 10. It appears on the stack in both lines, so total = 40 + 10 = 50.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Why a finished store is not yet durable
question: A server has ADR but not eADR. You map a file on a DAX file system with MAP_SHARED_VALIDATE | MAP_SYNC. Which granularity does libpmem2 report for the mapping?
options: PMEM2_GRANULARITY_CACHE_LINE: flush the touched cache lines, then fence
PMEM2_GRANULARITY_PAGE: you still need msync for durability
PMEM2_GRANULARITY_BYTE: every retired store is already durable
It depends on whether you use CLWB or CLFLUSHOPT
explain: MAP_SYNC succeeded, so the mapping is real persistent memory and PAGE is not needed. Without eADR the caches are outside the protected domain, so the result is CACHE_LINE. BYTE requires the persistence_domain to include cpu_cache. The flush instruction choice does not change the granularity.

courseTitle: Persistent memory data structures: crash consistency per cache line
lessonTitle: Concurrent PM indexes, RECIPE and what Optane measurements showed
question: A lock-free DRAM B+ tree's writers complete any half-finished split they encounter before doing their own work. Which RECIPE condition fits, and what does conversion need?
options: Condition #1: flush and fence after each store only
Condition #3: add a helper mechanism, then flushes and fences
Condition #2: add flushes and fences after stores, and after loads so observed state is persisted first
It cannot be converted, because lock-free indexes never satisfy RECIPE's conditions
explain: Writers that fix inconsistencies they find are Condition #2, like BwTree. The helper already exists, so recovery after a crash is just another writer finishing the job; conversion adds flushes and fences after stores and loads.

courseTitle: Pointers, memory layout, struct padding and alignment
lessonTitle: Overriding the rules: packed, alignas and unaligned data
question: Which is the right tool to give each of 8 per-thread counters its own 64-byte region in a static array?
options: __attribute__((packed)) on the counter struct
alignas(64) on the counter field (or Rust #[repr(align(64))])
Sorting the fields by alignment
Casting the array to char *
explain: Raising the alignment to 64 makes sizeof a multiple of 64, so every array element starts on a 64-byte boundary. Packing does the opposite and reordering cannot add space.

courseTitle: Pose estimation: heatmaps, grouping, OKS and joint angles
lessonTitle: Scoring poses with Object Keypoint Similarity
question: In the worked example the wrist's ground truth is changed to v = 0 (not labeled). What happens to OKS?
options: It stays 0.721, since prediction quality did not change
It drops, because a keypoint is now missing
It rises to 0.790, the mean of the other four similarities
It becomes undefined
explain: Unlabeled ground-truth keypoints are removed from both numerator and denominator. Dropping the worst term (0.444) leaves (0.598 + 0.800 + 0.929 + 0.832) / 4 = 0.790.

courseTitle: Pre-filtering vs post-filtering with metadata
lessonTitle: Filtering inside the graph walk, and when the graph falls apart
question: A strict filtered HNSW walk returns only 3 of the 10 requested results, all far from the query, even though 5,000 vectors match. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The 3 results are the true filtered nearest neighbors
Removing non-matching nodes split the graph, so the walk exhausted the matching fragment around the entry point
The allow list was computed incorrectly by the inverted index
ef is too large
explain: Five thousand matches exist, so a correct search would return 10. A strict walk can only reach matching nodes connected to its entry through matching nodes. Fixes: traverse through, add filter-aware edges (ACORN, Qdrant), seed matching entry points, or brute-force the matches.

courseTitle: Prefetching, memory bandwidth versus latency
lessonTitle: Hardware prefetchers: patterns, training and the page wall
question: You process particles in a loop and read only `x`, `y`, `z` of each. Which layout gives the hardware prefetcher the easiest job once the data exceeds the caches?
options: An array of 256-byte particle structs, reading three fields per struct
Separate dense arrays `x[]`, `y[]`, `z[]`
A linked list of particle structs allocated in loop order
A hash map from particle id to struct
explain: Dense arrays give three unit-stride streams where every byte fetched is used. The 256-byte structs also form a stride, but each 64-byte line fetched carries only the three fields you read (24 bytes if they are doubles), so most bytes moved are wasted. The list and hash map add dependent or scattered addresses.

courseTitle: Process reward models: grading reasoning one step at a time
lessonTitle: How a PRM is trained and how it scores a solution
question: Why did Lightman et al. surface 'convincing wrong-answer' solutions to labelers instead of random samples?
options: They are guaranteed to contain a step the current PRM misjudged, so each label corrects a real mistake
They are shorter, so labeling is cheaper
Random samples cannot be split into steps
It removes the need to label correct solutions at all
explain: A solution the PRM rates highly but whose answer is wrong must contain at least one step the PRM scored too high. Labeling it is maximally informative. This active learning was about 2.6x more data-efficient in their ablation.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: What a process owns and what a thread shares
question: A function stores a pointer to one of its local variables in a global, then returns. Another thread later dereferences that pointer. What is wrong?
options: Nothing: threads share the address space, so the local is still valid
The other thread cannot see the first thread's stack at all
The local lived on the first thread's stack frame, which was freed when the function returned, so the pointer now dangles
The kernel copies the local to the other thread's stack
explain: The memory is reachable (it is all one address space), but the stack frame is dead once the function returns and will be reused by later calls. Sharing the address space does not extend the lifetime of stack variables.

courseTitle: Processes, threads and the real cost of a context switch
lessonTitle: Counting switches and designing around them
question: A logging thread receives each log line from 16 worker threads through a mutex-protected queue and is woken for every line. At 200,000 lines per second, `voluntary_ctxt_switches` on the logger is enormous. Which fix targets the cause?
options: Give the logger a higher scheduling priority
Use more logging threads, one per worker
Batch: let workers append to a buffer and wake the logger once per batch (or every few milliseconds) instead of per line
Pin the logger to core 0
explain: Each line wakes the logger, which handles it and sleeps again: one voluntary switch per line on the logger, plus wakeup work for the workers. Batching turns 200,000 handoffs into a few hundred. More logging threads multiply the switches, and priority or pinning do not change how often they happen.

courseTitle: Product quantization (PQ)
lessonTitle: Code size vs recall, and refinements: OPQ, fast scan, ScaNN
question: A 4-bit fast-scan index (PQ32x4fs) and an 8-bit index (PQ16) both use 16 bytes per vector. Which statement matches the Faiss docs?
options: Fast scan is faster but less accurate than 8-bit PQ at the same memory, so pair it with re-ranking
They are identical because the bytes are equal
Fast scan is more accurate because it has more sub-quantizers
Fast scan stores float32 tables in registers
explain: Faiss notes 4-bit PQ is less accurate than 8-bit PQ for the same memory and recommends a refine stage. Its speed comes from 16-entry tables quantized to 8-bit integers, which fit in SIMD registers.

courseTitle: Protein design with diffusion over residue frames
lessonTitle: Sequence design, then the self-consistency check
question: Why does RFdiffusion run AlphaFold2 on the single designed sequence, with no multiple sequence alignment?
options: A designed sequence has no natural homologues, so an MSA would either be empty or misleading; single-sequence prediction is also the harder, more honest test
Because AF2 is faster without an MSA and the pipeline needs throughput
Because MSAs are only used for membrane proteins
Because the sequence is already known to be correct, so extra evidence would bias the result
explain: A de novo design is not a member of any natural protein family, so there is nothing meaningful to align it to. Running single-sequence prediction also means the model must fold the design from its own learned physics, which is a stricter test than letting it copy a homologue.

courseTitle: Query expansion: synonyms, feedback and LLM rewrites
lessonTitle: Synonym filters in Elasticsearch and OpenSearch
question: A rule `personal computer => pc` is used at search time. A user types `personal computer`; a document contains only `personal computer`, never `pc`. What happens?
options: It matches, because explicit rules keep both sides
It does not match through the synonym: the query is rewritten to pc, and the document was indexed without that rule
It matches only with expand: false
The analyzer rejects the rule because multi-word left sides are invalid
explain: An explicit rule replaces the left side with the right side. Applied only at search time, the query becomes pc, which this document does not contain. Use an equivalent rule (personal computer, pc) or include the original on the right side if both should match.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Conversational rewriting: turning a follow-up into a standalone query
question: In the toy, why did concatenating all three turns still rank the RAID disk document first?
options: Because BM25 ignores words from earlier turns
Because the disk document is the longest
Because concatenation removes the word raft
Because the concatenated query still contains happens and fails, which together match only the disk document
explain: Concatenation keeps every word of the current turn. happens appears only in d3, so it has a high IDF, and d3 matches both happens and fails. Adding raft and leader helps d2 but not enough to overtake it.

courseTitle: Query rewriting and decomposition
lessonTitle: Paying for it: latency, cost and when not to rewrite
question: Your rewriter makes 30% of first-turn queries slightly worse and adds 0.5 s to every request. Which change most directly addresses both problems?
options: Use a larger rewriter model
Generate 5 rewrites instead of 1
Concatenate the history instead of rewriting
Skip rewriting when the turn is already standalone (first turn, no unresolved references) and keep the original query otherwise as a fallback
explain: Gating removes the call where it adds no value (cutting latency) and avoids the drift it introduces on queries that were already fine. A larger model costs more time; more rewrites multiply drift; concatenation reintroduces stale-topic problems.

courseTitle: RaBitQ and binary quantization: 1-bit vectors with error bounds
lessonTitle: Computing the estimate with popcount, and re-ranking by the bound
question: Why can the error bound replace the usual 'rerank the top R candidates' hyperparameter?
options: The bound gives each candidate a lower bound on its distance, so you can skip exactly those that cannot beat the best exact distance found so far
The bound makes every estimate exact
The bound tells you the optimal R for each dataset ahead of time
Re-ranking is not needed for RaBitQ at all
explain: A fixed R must be tuned and can be too small on hard data (the paper shows no single R works across datasets). The bound adapts per query: easy queries re-rank few vectors, hard ones more.

courseTitle: Raft and Paxos consensus
lessonTitle: Raft leader election: terms, votes and randomized timeouts
question: Candidate S3 (term 7) is waiting for votes when it receives AppendEntries from S5 claiming to be leader of term 7. What should S3 do?
options: Recognize S5 as leader and return to follower state
Reject it, since S3 started its election first
Increment to term 8 and continue the election
Keep collecting votes; the server with more votes wins
explain: If the leader's term is at least as large as the candidate's term, the candidate accepts the leader as legitimate and steps down. S5 must already have a majority for term 7, so S3 cannot also win term 7.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Why an LLM needs a retriever: parametric vs non-parametric memory
question: In RAG-Sequence, what does the term $p_\eta(z \mid x)$ contribute?
options: The generator's probability of each answer token
The retriever's weight for passage z, so answers supported by higher-scoring passages count more
A penalty for long passages
The probability that the question is answerable
explain: The sum runs over the top k passages. Each term multiplies the retriever's probability for passage z by the generator's probability of the whole answer given z. The retriever acts as a soft selector over evidence.

courseTitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: the pipeline and its failures
lessonTitle: Evaluating retrieval and generation separately
question: Why is faithfulness alone not enough to evaluate a RAG system?
options: It needs a human-written reference answer
An answer can be fully faithful to retrieved context that is wrong, stale or irrelevant, and can say I do not know faithfully
It only works for single-sentence answers
It rewards answers that cite many sources
explain: Faithfulness compares the answer to the context, not to the truth or to the question. Pair it with answer relevance and with retrieval metrics. Ragas faithfulness needs no reference answer, which is part of its appeal.

courseTitle: Feature engineering for ranking
lessonTitle: Document, query and interaction signals: freshness, popularity, clicks
question: A news ranker uses linear freshness with maxAge 90 days. Editors complain that a 2-hour-old story and a 2-day-old story look the same to the model. What change best fixes this?
options: Use a logscale freshness with a small halfResponse such as 1 day
Increase maxAge to 365 days
Drop freshness and rely on popularity
Use raw age in seconds without transformation
explain: Linear freshness drops only 1/90 per day, so 2 hours and 2 days differ by about 0.02. A logscale curve with halfResponse 1 day spends most of its range in the first days. Raising maxAge makes the slope even flatter.

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Cutoff metrics and the divisors hidden inside them
question: Library X reports MAP@10 = 0.41 and library Y reports MAP@10 = 0.47 on the same run and qrels. Neither has a bug. What is the most likely cause?
options: Y divides each query's AP sum by min(R, 10) while X divides by R
X uses log base 2 and Y uses natural log
X averages over queries and Y over documents
Y uses exponential gain
explain: AP has no log or gain. Dividing by min(R, k) instead of R raises every query whose R exceeds k, so Y comes out higher. The trec_eval convention divides by all relevant documents R; the Kaggle ml_metrics apk divides by min(R, k).

courseTitle: Ranking metrics: precision@k, recall@k, NDCG, MRR
lessonTitle: Is the difference real? Paired tests, effect sizes, many systems
question: Two systems have per-query nDCG differences that are tiny but positive on 980 of 1000 queries. A paired t-test gives p < 0.0001. What is the right reading?
options: B is much better than A
The test is invalid with 1000 queries
B is reliably better, but the effect may be too small to matter; report the mean difference and its confidence interval
Use a sign test instead because the differences are small
