explain: With many topics, the t statistic grows with the square root of n, so tiny consistent differences become highly significant. Significance says the difference is probably real, not that it is large. Sakai recommends reporting effect sizes and confidence intervals so readers can judge the magnitude.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Memory registration: pinning, translation and keys
question: `ibv_reg_mr(pd, buf, len, IBV_ACCESS_REMOTE_WRITE)` returns NULL. Most likely cause?
options: Remote write requires IBV_ACCESS_REMOTE_READ
The buffer must be registered by the peer, not locally
Remote write is only allowed on UD QPs
Remote write also requires IBV_ACCESS_LOCAL_WRITE
explain: The ibv_reg_mr man page states that if IBV_ACCESS_REMOTE_WRITE or IBV_ACCESS_REMOTE_ATOMIC is set, IBV_ACCESS_LOCAL_WRITE must be set too. Remote read is independent, and UD QPs do not support RDMA WRITE at all.

courseTitle: RDMA: kernel-bypass networking with verbs
lessonTitle: Scaling RDMA: NIC caches, doorbells, timeouts and failure
question: You post 16 small WRITEs per loop iteration, each with its own `ibv_post_send` call. Which change most directly reduces CPU MMIO work?
options: Make every WR signaled
Chain the 16 WRs in one linked list and post them with a single call so one doorbell covers them
Use RDMA READ instead
Increase the CQ size
explain: ibv_post_send accepts a linked list of WRs. Posting them together lets the driver ring one doorbell and have the NIC fetch all WQEs by DMA (Doorbell batching), instead of one MMIO sequence per WR. Signaling every WR adds CQE writes instead of removing work.

courseTitle: Real-time multiplayer networking: WebSockets and state sync
lessonTitle: Showing other players: interpolation and lag compensation
question: After adding lag compensation, players complain they get shot just after diving behind cover. What is happening?
options: The server is validating the shot against the shooter's slightly older view, where the target was still exposed
A bug in interpolation on the target's client
The target's prediction is wrong
TCP retransmission delayed the hit message
explain: This is the documented tradeoff: hits are judged in the shooter's past. Gambetta calls it somewhat unfair but the most agreeable option, since missing a shot that was dead-on from your own screen feels worse.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Implicit feedback: preference, confidence and weighted ALS
question: In Hu et al.'s model, what does a cell with r_ui = 0 contribute to the loss?
options: Nothing: unobserved cells are skipped, as in explicit matrix factorization
A strong push toward a negative rating of -1
A term with target p = 0 and minimum confidence c = 1, a weak signal that u probably does not prefer i
A term whose weight is set by the item's popularity
explain: With c = 1 + alpha r, a zero count gives c = 1: the cell is in the loss with target 0 but much less weight than observed events, reflecting that a missing event has many possible causes.

courseTitle: Recommender systems and cold start
lessonTitle: Evaluating recommenders without fooling yourself
question: In Hu et al.'s TV evaluation, why were shows the user had already watched in training removed from the test set?
options: People rewatch the same shows weekly, so predicting them is easy and would inflate the score without testing discovery
They were too rare to matter
They made the percentile ranking undefined
The confidence weights for them were zero
explain: Hu et al. note the tendency to repeatedly watch the same programs and remove these 'easy' predictions so the evaluation measures recommending something new.

courseTitle: Relational operators: joins, aggregation and planning
lessonTitle: When each join wins: row counts, probes and memory
question: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows a Hash node with `Batches: 16`. What does that tell you?
options: The hash table had 16 buckets
The build side did not fit in hash memory, so both inputs were split and partly written to temp files
The join ran on 16 parallel workers
The planner tried 16 join orders
explain: Batches count partitions of the hash join. More than one means the inner input exceeded work_mem x hash_mem_multiplier, so rows of later batches were written to and reread from disk. Remedies: give the operation more memory, build on a smaller input, or filter rows earlier.

courseTitle: Replication and quorums: N, R, W and what they really buy you
lessonTitle: Leaderless quorums: why R + W > N makes reads overlap writes
question: N = 3. A service needs reads to see the latest completed write and must keep accepting writes when one replica is down. Which (R, W) fits?
explain: R + W must exceed 3, and W must be at most 3 - 1 = 2 to tolerate one dead replica. Only R = 2, W = 2 satisfies both. R = 1, W = 3 overlaps but blocks writes on any failure; the other two do not overlap.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When a high score stops meaning a solved task
question: A chat model is trained against a reward model that, on the SFT model's outputs, gave slightly higher scores to longer answers because longer answers were usually more complete. After heavy RL, answers are very long and padded. Which cause from Amodei et al. fits best?
options: Goodhart's law: a correlation that held under normal outputs broke under strong optimization
Environmental embedding: the model tampered with the reward computation
Partially observed goals: the model cannot see the user
The RL algorithm diverged because the learning rate was too high
explain: Length correlated with quality on ordinary outputs, so it looked like a fine signal. Optimizing hard pushed the policy to outputs where the correlation no longer holds. Nothing touched the reward code (not wireheading), and a training instability would not produce this systematic, high-scoring behavior.

courseTitle: Reward hacking: when optimizing the score breaks the task
lessonTitle: When the verifier is code: test hacking in coding agents
question: In a GRPO group, all 4 rollouts use the same hack and all get reward 1. What is the advantage of each, and what does that imply?
options: 0 each (zero variance), so this group adds no gradient; the hack was already reinforced when it competed with honest failures
+1 each, so the hack is reinforced as strongly as ever
-1 each, so GRPO automatically corrects saturated hacks
Undefined, so training crashes
explain: All rewards equal the mean, so every advantage is 0 (implementations add a small epsilon to the standard deviation to avoid dividing by zero). Saturated groups stop teaching anything, including how to solve the task honestly. The damage happened earlier, in mixed groups where the hack stood out.

courseTitle: RL post-training infrastructure at scale
lessonTitle: Weight sync: resharding and moving the bytes every step
question: Training uses TP 8, and generation could reuse TP 8 (the setting HybridFlow attributes to NeMo-Aligner). Why might a system still choose to reshard to TP 2 for generation, despite the transition cost?
options: TP 2 uses less weight-sync bandwidth across the network
Larger TP is not supported by vLLM
Resharding makes the weights smaller
Generation is memory-bound; fewer shards per replica means more independent replicas, each decoding a large batch, and HybridFlow measured 60.3% lower generation latency for 7B at TP 2
explain: With TP 8 a 7B model's decode steps are tiny per GPU and spend time on communication. Smaller TP gives 4x more independent replicas with large batches. HybridFlow found TP 2 best for 7B; going lower failed to help because a smaller TP needs more KV cache per GPU.

courseTitle: Roofline model and GPU bandwidth measurement
lessonTitle: Placing GEMM, softmax and LLM decode on the roofline
question: A serving team raises decode batch size from 8 to 64 on a 4096-wide BF16 layer on an H100. Roughly what happens to the time per decode step for that layer?
options: It grows about 8x because there is 8x more math
It halves because Tensor Cores are used more efficiently
It grows about 64x because each token needs its own weight read
It stays nearly the same, because the step is still bound by reading the weights
explain: At batch 8 and 64 the layer is far left of the ridge (intensity about 8 and 62). Time is set by streaming 33.6 MB of weights, which is the same for both batches. Throughput rises almost 8x for free, which is why servers batch decode requests.

courseTitle: Root cause analysis: from correlated alerts to the actual cause
lessonTitle: What touched it last: change correlation and bisection
question: Changes are rare (about one per three hours in the relevant subsystem) and your metric broke 12 seconds after a config push. Which statement is accurate?
options: The near-coincidence is unlikely by chance, so the push is now the leading hypothesis and should be tested by reverting it or reproducing its effect
The 12 second gap proves causation, since the expected number of unrelated changes per minute is 0.0055
The gap is too short: a real config change takes minutes to propagate, so this must be something else
The push can be dismissed, because the first alert did not fire until two minutes later
explain: Rarity makes the coincidence informative, not conclusive: it promotes the push to the leading hypothesis, which you then test by mechanism (does a pool of 4 saturate at 360 rps?) and by reverting. Rarity bounds coincidence; it does not establish a mechanism, so the option claiming proof overclaims. The 12 second gap is what the model predicts for the queue to fill, and alert delay is a property of your alerting window.

courseTitle: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
lessonTitle: RRF next to CombSUM, CombMNZ, Borda and Condorcet
question: You replace every BM25 score by its square root before fusing (same order). Which fused list can change?
options: RRF
Borda
CombSUM on min-max normalized scores
Condorcet
explain: A square root preserves order, so all rank-based methods are unaffected. Min-max scaling is linear, so after a non-linear transform the normalized values, and therefore the sums, change. Score fusion is sensitive to how scores are shaped, not only to their order.

courseTitle: Rust in the Linux kernel: safe abstractions over unsafe C
lessonTitle: Locks and refcounts as types: Guard, Opaque and Arc
question: In C, a driver function takes a spinlock, calls a helper that returns an error, and returns early without unlocking. Which part of the Rust version prevents the equivalent bug?
options: The borrow checker forbids early returns while a lock is held
lockdep runs at compile time in Rust
The guard returned by `lock()` is dropped on every exit path, and its `Drop` calls the backend's unlock
Rust spinlocks are released automatically by the scheduler
explain: Early returns are allowed; they simply run destructors for live locals. `Guard::drop` calls `B::unlock`. lockdep still runs at runtime as in C; the Guard constructor even asserts the lock is held.

courseTitle: sched_ext: writing Linux CPU schedulers in eBPF
lessonTitle: Dispatch queues: how tasks travel from BPF to a CPU
question: CPU2's local DSQ is empty. The global DSQ holds task X (queued 1 ms ago) and custom DSQ 7 holds task Y (queued 50 ms ago). Which task does CPU2 run next, assuming no new insertions?
options: Y, because it has waited longer and DSQs are served oldest first across queues
X, because the global DSQ is consumed before ops.dispatch() is ever called
Y, because custom DSQs have priority over built-in ones
Neither until ops.dispatch() chooses between them
explain: The pick order is fixed: local DSQ, then global DSQ, then ops.dispatch(). X is taken from the global DSQ without consulting the BPF scheduler. Y only moves if ops.dispatch() later calls scx_bpf_dsq_move_to_local(7).

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Why a model can teach itself: improve, then distill
question: Why does training the policy head on MCTS visit counts improve the network instead of just copying it?
options: Visit counts are smoother than the prior, so the cross-entropy loss is lower
The search samples at a higher temperature, so the targets are more diverse
The search mixes the prior with measured look-ahead values, so the visit counts differ from the prior where look-ahead finds better moves
The visit counts include moves from human expert games
explain: The search is an improvement operator: it starts from the prior and moves visits toward moves whose measured values are higher. In the toy, the prior said 0.30 for b and the search said 0.889. Imitating that difference is the improvement. AlphaZero uses no human games.

courseTitle: Self-play and self-improvement: how models learn from their own output
lessonTitle: Inventing the tasks: Absolute Zero and what bounds every loop
question: An Absolute Zero proposer writes a program that calls random.random() and returns the result. What happens to this proposal?
options: It becomes a hard abduction task, so the proposer gets a high learnability reward
It fails validation (random is a forbidden module, and two runs would give different outputs anyway), so it counts as a formatting error with reward -1
The solver gets credit for any numeric answer between 0 and 1
It is accepted, but only as an induction task
explain: Absolute Zero only accepts deterministic programs: it bans modules such as random and datetime outright, and it also runs each program twice (j = 2) and compares outputs. Only proposals that produce valid triplets count as correctly formatted, so this one gets the -1 penalty, which teaches the proposer to avoid unverifiable tasks.

courseTitle: SGLang: RadixAttention, cache-aware scheduling, compressed FSMs
lessonTitle: Inside the server: three processes and an overlapped loop
question: Your server runs out of GPU memory during prefill of very long prompts, while decoding is fine. Which change do the docs suggest first?
options: Disable the radix cache
Switch the schedule policy to lpm
Lower `--chunked-prefill-size` (for example to 4096 or 2048)
Increase `--mem-fraction-static`
explain: Prefill activations scale with the number of tokens in one forward pass, and chunking caps it. Raising `--mem-fraction-static` would give the KV pool more memory and leave less for activations, making prefill OOM more likely.

courseTitle: Shortest-path routing on road graphs
lessonTitle: Bidirectional search and contraction hierarchies
question: While contracting v, the path u, v, w costs 8, and a witness search finds a path from u to w avoiding v that also costs 8. What should the preprocessing do?
options: Add the shortcut, because ties must be preserved
Add the shortcut with weight 7 to prefer it
Abort the contraction of v
Skip the shortcut; an equally short path survives without v
explain: A shortcut is only needed when the path through v is the unique shortest path. An equally short witness keeps dist(u, w) correct in the remaining graph. In the toy, contracting G found a witness for D to T that is even shorter (the shortcut of weight 7 beats 8), so no shortcut was added there either.

courseTitle: Signal processing basics: sampling, the FFT and filters
lessonTitle: Frequency bins, resolution and spectral leakage
question: Audio at 48000 Hz is analyzed with a 4096-point FFT. What is the spacing between frequency bins?
options: About 11.7 Hz
About 0.085 Hz
explain: Bin spacing is fs/N = 48000/4096 = 11.71875 Hz. 24000 Hz is the Nyquist frequency (the last rfft bin), not the spacing. A 4096-sample block lasts about 85 ms, and the spacing is the inverse of that duration.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Writing a vector loop: intrinsics, reductions and tails
question: Clang will not vectorize `for (...) s += a[i];` over floats at -O2, but does vectorize the same loop over ints. Why?
options: Integer SIMD registers are wider
Floats cannot be loaded with vector loads
The loop has an aliasing problem only for floats
Vectorizing changes the order of additions, which changes float rounding but not integer results
explain: Wraparound integer addition is associative, so any order gives the same bits. Float addition rounds at every step, so reordering can change the result, and the compiler needs -ffast-math, -fassociative-math or a pragma to allow it.

courseTitle: SIMD: AVX2, AVX-512, Arm Neon and SVE from the lanes up
lessonTitle: Shipping SIMD: -march levels, runtime dispatch, portability
question: In the Rust example, why is `sum_avx2` marked `unsafe`?
options: It dereferences raw pointers
AVX2 instructions are memory-unsafe
Rust forbids SIMD in safe code
Calling it on a CPU without AVX2 would execute unsupported instructions, so the caller must guarantee the feature
explain: The std::arch docs explain that #[target_feature] functions can only be correctly called on systems with that feature, so calling them is unsafe; the is_x86_feature_detected! check is what makes the call sound.

courseTitle: Slab, bump/arena and buddy allocators
lessonTitle: The slab allocator: caches of ready-made objects
question: Why can the slab allocator reclaim memory without the coalescing step a buddy allocator needs?
options: Because it never returns memory to the system
Because objects are always freed in the order they were allocated
Because a slab is a whole page-sized unit with a refcount: when the count reaches zero the entire slab goes back, no matter where its neighbors are
Because slab objects are always 2^k bytes and aligned like buddies
explain: The slab, not the object, is the unit exchanged with the page allocator. Freeing an object only decrements its slab's count; when it hits zero the slab's pages return in one step.

courseTitle: slime: RL post-training with Megatron and SGLang
lessonTitle: Moving weights from Megatron into SGLang
question: Your trainer runs with PP=4. In the NCCL path, how many weight-update process groups are created, and who sends in each?
options: One group; global rank 0 gathers everything and sends
One group per engine; every training rank sends its own shard
Four groups, one per pipeline stage; that stage's DP-rank-0, TP-rank-0 rank broadcasts its layers
No groups; SGLang pulls from Megatron's checkpoint
explain: Each pipeline stage holds different layers, so slime creates a group per stage (`slime-pp_{rank}`), and the stage's source rank (data-parallel rank 0, tensor-parallel rank 0) broadcasts full tensors after the TP and EP gathers.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: The sparse autoencoder: a wide, sparse dictionary for activations
question: Why does Scaling Monosemanticity multiply each latent's activation by its decoder norm inside the sparsity penalty?
options: To make the encoder run faster
So the SAE cannot lower the penalty by shrinking activations while growing decoder columns, which would leave reconstructions unchanged
To force exactly k latents to be active
Because decoder norms equal the language model's loss
explain: Scaling f_i down by c and d_i up by c leaves f_i d_i (and so x-hat) unchanged but cuts a plain L1 penalty by c. Weighting by the decoder norm makes the penalty invariant to that rescaling. A unit-norm constraint on decoder columns achieves the same thing.

courseTitle: Sparse autoencoders: pulling features out of superposition
lessonTitle: Measuring an SAE and steering a model with its features
question: You clamp a latent to a large negative value although the encoder never outputs negatives. What happens to the activation?
options: Nothing; negative clamps are clipped to zero
A negative multiple of the latent's decoder direction is added to x
The latent's decoder direction is deleted
All other latents are set to zero
explain: Scaling Monosemanticity notes that clamping to a negative value simply gives a negative multiple of the feature vector. In their code-error example, negative clamping made the model predict the output the code would have produced without the bug.

courseTitle: Spatial interpolation: IDW, variograms and kriging
lessonTitle: Kriging is Gaussian process regression in map coordinates
question: A data scientist fits a GP to sensor data with an RBF kernel plus a white noise kernel. In kriging vocabulary, the white noise variance corresponds to:
options: The range
The sill
The nugget
The Lagrange multiplier
explain: A white noise term adds variance only on the diagonal, exactly like a nugget: semivariance jumps from 0 to the nugget as soon as two points are distinct.

courseTitle: Speculative decoding: draft fast, verify in one pass, lose nothing
lessonTitle: Speculative sampling: guesses that keep the target's distribution
question: Which pair of models has the higher acceptance rate beta for a single position?
options: Both are equal because both drafts put most mass on the first token
explain: beta = sum of min(p, q). First pair: 0.5 + 0.1 = 0.6. Second pair: 0.5 + 0.4 = 0.9. What matters is overlap with the target, not agreeing on the top token.

courseTitle: Speech-to-text: log-mel features, Whisper, CTC and WER
lessonTitle: Whisper: a transformer over 30-second spectrogram windows
question: You pass 12 s of audio to Whisper. What does the encoder process?
options: A 80 x 1200 spectrogram, 600 positions
A 80 x 3000 spectrogram, 1500 positions, with the last 18 s padded with zeros
Three 4 s chunks processed in parallel
The raw 192,000 samples directly
explain: Whisper always feeds the encoder 30 s: the low-level API pads the audio to 480,000 samples, and `transcribe` pads each log-mel window to 3000 frames, so the shape is always 80 x 3000 and the stem always yields 1500 positions. The padded tail is silence, which matters later when we look at hallucinations.

courseTitle: Stack vs heap, virtual memory, paging and TLB
lessonTitle: The stack: memory that frees itself when a function returns
question: A function returns `&x`, where `x` is one of its local variables. The caller reads the pointer immediately and gets the right value, but after calling `printf` it reads garbage. Why?
options: The compiler moved x to the heap, and printf freed it
x's frame was released on return; printf's own frame reused those stack bytes
Reading a stack variable from another function always raises SIGSEGV
The red zone is cleared by the kernel on every return
explain: Returning only moves `rsp` back up; the bytes are not erased, so an immediate read may look fine. The next call (here `printf`) pushes its frame into the same addresses and overwrites them. No fault occurs because the memory is still mapped, which is what makes this bug so sneaky. The red zone is never cleared by the kernel.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Steering by adding a vector to the residual stream
question: Why can a vector added only at layer l change the model's next-token prediction?
options: Because the model recomputes all earlier layers after the addition
Because the residual stream is a running sum: later layers read the shifted stream and the unembedding reads its final value
Because the vector is also added to the weights of every later layer
It cannot; the vector must be added at the last layer to matter
explain: Each block adds its output to the stream it reads, so a vector added at layer l stays in the sum. Later attention and MLP layers read it and react to it, and the final stream is what the unembedding decodes. No weights change and earlier layers are not rerun.

courseTitle: Steering vectors and activation engineering
lessonTitle: Side effects and how to evaluate a steering vector
question: Your refusal-steered model keeps its MMLU score, yet users report rambling, repetitive answers. Which check would have caught this?
options: Raising the coefficient
Measuring loss or KL on ordinary prompts and reading open-ended generations, not just multiple-choice accuracy
Running MMLU with more subjects
Using a single contrast pair instead of many
explain: MMLU in the A/B format reads one token's probability, which can survive while generation quality collapses. CAA saw exactly this: multiple-choice capability held while larger multipliers degraded open-ended text. Loss on ordinary text, KL on unrelated prompts and reading samples catch it.

courseTitle: Streaming sensor pipelines: event time, watermarks, online filters
lessonTitle: Online filtering: EMA as a low-pass, Welford for anomaly flags
question: Two parallel tasks each computed Welford state for half of a sensor's readings. Can you get the exact overall variance?
options: No, variance needs all raw values in one place
Yes, by averaging the two variances
Yes, by combining (n, mean, M2) of both halves with a pairwise merge formula
Only if both halves have the same mean
explain: Averaging variances ignores the difference between the two means. Chan, Golub and LeVeque give a merge: M2 = M2a + M2b + delta squared x na x nb / (na + nb), with delta the difference of means. This is what makes mean and variance easy to parallelize across partitions.

courseTitle: Attention and the Transformer
lessonTitle: Causal masks, cross-attention and multiple heads
question: A bug report: a decoder trains to near-zero loss quickly, but generates garbage at inference. Which bug is most likely?
options: The scale factor uses d_model instead of d_k
The causal mask is missing, so during training each position could read the token it was supposed to predict
The model uses 8 heads instead of 1
The softmax is applied over columns instead of rows
explain: With teacher forcing the whole target is fed in at once. Without the causal mask, position i can attend to position i+1 (its own answer), so training is trivially easy. At inference those future tokens do not exist yet, and the model has never learned to predict without them.

courseTitle: BM25: saturating, length-normalized term weighting
lessonTitle: Term-frequency saturation: what k1 controls
question: With k1 = 1.2 and average-length documents, doc P contains a term 2 times and doc Q contains it 20 times. Roughly how much larger is Q's factor than P's?
options: About 1.5 times larger (0.94 vs 0.62)
10 times larger
Exactly the same
About 3 times larger
explain: P: 2/(2+1.2) = 0.625. Q: 20/(21.2) = 0.943. The ratio is about 1.5, not 10. That is saturation: ten times the count gives about one and a half times the weight.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Causal self-attention: each position may only look backward
question: A bug report: the mask was built with `torch.triu(torch.ones(T, T))` instead of `torch.tril(...)`, keeping the `masked_fill(mask == 0, -inf)` line unchanged. What does position 0 attend to now?
options: Only itself, as before
All positions 0 to T-1, including the future
Nothing, so its row is all minus infinity
Only position T-1
explain: triu keeps the upper triangle, so row 0 keeps columns 0 to T-1 and the model sees the whole future from the first position. The last row is the one that keeps just one key, its own. The loss will look great and generation will fail.

courseTitle: Build a GPT from scratch
lessonTitle: Generating text: the sampling loop, temperature and top-k
question: A sampling script uses `logits[logits <= v[:, [-1]]] = -inf` (note `<=`) with top_k = 5. What happens?
options: Nothing changes; < and <= behave the same
The 5th-largest logit (and any ties with it) is also removed, so only 4 tokens survive; with top_k = 1 every logit is masked and softmax returns NaN
Top-k now keeps 6 tokens
Temperature stops having an effect
explain: v[:, [-1]] is the k-th largest logit, the threshold that must survive. With <= it is thrown away too, leaving k - 1 choices, and for k = 1 nothing survives: all minus infinity gives NaN probabilities and multinomial fails.

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: What happens when you press Enter: lookup, fork, exec, wait
question: A script `setup.sh` contains `cd build` and `export MODE=dev`. You run it as `./setup.sh`, then type `pwd`. What do you see?
options: Your original directory, and MODE is unset in your shell
The build directory, because the script changed into it
The build directory, but MODE is unset because export only affects children
An error, because cd is a builtin and cannot run in a script
explain: `./setup.sh` runs in a child bash process. Its cd and export change only that child, which then exits. To apply them to your current shell you must run the file inside it with `source setup.sh` (or `. setup.sh`).

courseTitle: Command line, shell and tooling: how bash really runs your commands
lessonTitle: Exit statuses and scripts that fail loudly
question: A script has `set -e`. Its line `grep -q TODO notes.txt && echo found` runs when notes.txt has no TODO. What happens?
options: The script exits with status 1 because grep failed
Nothing prints and the script continues with the next line
The script exits with status 127
The echo runs because && ignores failures under -e
explain: grep is not the final command of the `&&` list, so its failure is exempt from -e. The echo is skipped and execution continues. (If this were the last line, the script's own exit status would still be 1.)

courseTitle: Embeddings and representation learning: from IDs to vectors
lessonTitle: What the geometry means: cosine, analogies and PMI
question: Your search for words similar to *cheap* returns *expensive* near the top. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Antonyms share most of their contexts (prices, tickets, very), so distributional training places them close
A bug: cosine similarity must be negative for antonyms
The vectors were not normalized before training
Negative sampling inverts antonym vectors
explain: The objective only sees contexts. *Cheap* and *expensive* appear around the same words, so their vectors align. Nothing in SGNS or GloVe pushes antonyms to negative cosine.

courseTitle: GPU and inference basics
lessonTitle: Prefill and decode: FLOPs and bytes per generated token
question: Which change most reduces time to first token for a request with a very long prompt?
options: Faster HBM only
More math throughput (or splitting prefill across GPUs), since prefill is compute-bound
A larger decode batch
Lowering the number of output tokens
explain: TTFT is dominated by prefill (plus any queueing), and prefill of many tokens is compute-bound. Output length affects total latency, not TTFT.

courseTitle: How a computer runs a program
lessonTitle: Where a program's memory lives: code, heap and stack
question: Why does sumsq copy b into rbx before calling square, instead of leaving it in rsi?
options: Because rsi is reserved for return values
Because square may overwrite rsi freely, while the ABI requires square to preserve rbx
Because rbx is faster than rsi
Because the stack is full
explain: The System V ABI splits registers into caller-saved ones (like rdi, rsi, rax) that any callee may clobber, and callee-saved ones (rbx, rbp, r12 to r15) that a callee must restore before returning. That is also why sumsq itself pushes rbx and r14 first: it is about to use them and must hand them back intact.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: From text predictor to assistant: the three-stage recipe
question: A base model is given the prompt "Write a haiku about rain." Why might it fail to write a haiku?
options: It continues the text as a plausible document, which may be more instructions or a list of prompts rather than an answer
Its weights contain no knowledge of poetry, which only SFT adds
Base models cannot generate text without a reward model
The prompt is too short for the attention mechanism
explain: Pretraining optimizes next-token likelihood on documents. A line like this often appears in lists of writing prompts, so continuing with more prompts is a likely continuation. The knowledge of haiku is already in the base model; SFT and RLHF teach it to respond as an assistant.

courseTitle: How LLMs are trained: pretraining, SFT, RLHF
lessonTitle: RL with PPO: maximize reward, stay close to the SFT model
question: During RLHF, the mean reward keeps rising while the KL from the SFT model shoots up and samples start repeating odd phrases. Which change most directly addresses this?
options: Raise beta, or stop at an earlier checkpoint
Lower beta so the policy can explore more
Lower the PPO clip range to 0
Remove the value model
explain: Rising reward with exploding KL is the signature of the policy exploiting the reward model. A larger beta makes drift more expensive, and earlier checkpoints have less drift. Lowering beta makes it worse; a clip range of 0 stops learning entirely.

courseTitle: Inverted indexes and TF-IDF: how keyword search works
lessonTitle: Answering AND queries by merging postings
question: You intersect a 10-entry list with a 1,000,000-entry list using the plain two-pointer merge. Roughly how many steps can it take in the worst case?
options: About 10, because the result has at most 10 documents
About 20, because each short entry costs two comparisons
About 1,000,000, because the pointer may have to walk the long list nearly to its end
About log2(1,000,000) = 20 per entry, because the lists are sorted
explain: The plain merge advances one step at a time, so in the worst case it walks the whole long list: O(x + y). Doing about 20 steps per short entry is what you get only if you add skips or binary search into the long list, which the plain merge does not do.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: From main.c to a running program: the four toolchain stages
question: Your build prints "undefined reference to `area'". `main.c` already has `#include "square.h"`, which declares `area`. What is the most likely fix?
options: Add another #include "square.h" to area.c
Pass area.c (or area.o) to the link command
Compile main.c with -O2 so the call is inlined
Add the -E flag so the macro is expanded
explain: This message comes from the linker: main.o refers to the symbol area but no object file or library on the command line defines it. Headers only declare. The fix is to give the linker the definition, for example `gcc main.c area.c -o app`.

courseTitle: Learn C: pointers, memory and the toolchain
lessonTitle: Undefined behavior, and the tools that catch it
question: Which of these operations has fully defined behavior in standard C?
options: int x = INT_MAX; x = x + 1;
unsigned u = UINT_MAX; u = u + 1;
int a[5]; int y = a[5];
free(p); free(p);
explain: Unsigned arithmetic wraps modulo 2 to the power of the bit width, so u becomes 0. Signed overflow, reading one past the end of an array, and freeing twice are all undefined behavior.

courseTitle: Rust ownership and borrowing: memory safety without free() or a GC
lessonTitle: Borrowing: many readers or one writer
question: A colleague says the Vec error is pointless in single-threaded code because no other thread can touch `v`. What is the best reply?
options: They are right; the check only matters with threads
`push` may reallocate and free the old buffer, so `first` could dangle even with one thread
`push` always copies the vector, so `first` becomes stale but still safe to read
explain: Reallocation frees the old block, so the shared reference could point at freed memory: a use after free with no threads involved. `push` only reallocates when length equals capacity, which is exactly why the danger is easy to miss in testing.

courseTitle: Linear algebra intuition: vectors, dot products and matrices
lessonTitle: The dot product: one number that measures alignment
question: Two unit vectors have a dot product of 0.5. What is the angle between them?
options: 30 degrees
60 degrees
45 degrees
It depends on their dimension
explain: For unit vectors the dot product equals $\cos\theta$, and $\cos 60^\circ = 0.5$. The formula holds in any dimension, because any two vectors span a flat plane in which the angle is measured.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Loss: turning "fits the data" into one number
question: A classifier gives the correct class probability 0.9 on one example and 0.1 on another. Roughly how do their cross-entropy losses compare?
options: The 0.1 example costs about 22 times more (2.303 vs 0.105)
They are equal, since both are 0.4 away from 0.5
The 0.1 example costs exactly 9 times more
The 0.9 example costs more because it is more confident
explain: Cross-entropy is $-\ln p$: $-\ln 0.9 = 0.105$ and $-\ln 0.1 = 2.303$, a ratio of about 22. The log makes the cost grow without bound as the probability of the right answer goes to 0, which is exactly the confident-wrong case.

courseTitle: ML fundamentals: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
lessonTitle: Fighting overfitting: validation, weight decay, early stopping
question: With SGD and learning rate 0.1, an L2 term $\lambda\lVert w\rVert^2$ with $\lambda = 0.0005$ shrinks each weight by what factor before the gradient step?
explain: The step is $w \leftarrow (1 - 2\eta\lambda)w - \eta\nabla L$, and $2 \times 0.1 \times 0.0005 = 0.0001$, so the factor is $0.9999$. Note the factor 2 from differentiating $\lambda w^2$; many libraries define the penalty with a $\tfrac{1}{2}$ to cancel it.

courseTitle: Neural networks and backpropagation
lessonTitle: Backprop in practice: cost, memory, vanishing gradients
question: A training loop calls `loss.backward()` and `opt.step()` every iteration but never calls `opt.zero_grad()`. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, backward overwrites .grad each time
Each step uses the sum of all gradients so far, so updates grow and point in stale directions
The graph is freed, so the second backward raises an error
Weights stop changing after the first step
explain: PyTorch accumulates into `.grad` (the `+=` rule for forks, applied across calls). Without zeroing, step t applies the sum of gradients from steps 1 to t. The official tutorial calls zero_grad every iteration to avoid this double counting.

courseTitle: Operating systems basics: the three easy pieces of OSTEP
lessonTitle: Concurrency: race conditions and locks
question: On a single CPU with a non-preemptive scheduler (no timer switches), Thread 2 calls a spin lock held by Thread 1. What happens?
options: Thread 2 acquires the lock after one time slice
Thread 2 spins forever: Thread 1 never gets the CPU back to release the lock
The lock automatically turns into a sleeping lock
Thread 1 releases the lock because spinning causes an interrupt
explain: A spinning thread never gives up the CPU on its own. Without preemption, the holder never runs again, so the lock is never released. OSTEP points out that spin locks need a preemptive scheduler to work correctly on a single processor.

courseTitle: Probability and statistics basics for machine learning
lessonTitle: Random variables, expected value and variance
question: X is a die roll and Y = 7 - X (the face on the opposite side). What is Var(X + Y)?
options: Undefined, because X and Y are dependent
explain: X + Y = 7 always, a constant, so its variance is 0. Adding the variances (35/6) would be wrong because X and Y are perfectly negatively correlated, and the covariance term cancels them exactly. Linearity still gives E[X + Y] = 7.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Why loss falls on a straight line in log-log space
question: On log-log axes, a team's loss-versus-parameters points lie on a straight line with slope -0.07. Which statement is correct?
options: Each doubling of N removes the same fraction of the loss
Each doubling of N removes the same absolute amount of loss
Loss will reach zero at a finite model size
The slope says how much data the model needs
explain: A straight line in log-log space is a power law: equal multiplicative steps in N give equal multiplicative changes in L, here $2^{-0.07} \approx 0.95$ per doubling. Absolute drops shrink, the curve never reaches zero, and the slope says nothing about data needs on its own.

courseTitle: Scaling laws: predicting loss from model size, data and compute
lessonTitle: Inference cost, overtraining and where scaling laws break
question: Exact-match accuracy on a task jumps from near 0% to 60% between two model sizes, while per-token loss falls smoothly. What is the most careful reading?
options: The larger model suddenly acquired a new capability that scaling laws cannot describe
The metric is nonlinear: smooth per-token gains compound into an all-or-nothing score, so the jump may be partly a metric effect
The loss measurement must be wrong
The smaller model was undertrained, which fully explains the jump
explain: Schaeffer et al. show that discontinuous metrics like exact match can turn smooth improvement into apparent jumps, and continuous metrics make the trend smooth again. That is why Llama 3 forecast accuracy through NLL first. It does not prove no real change ever happens, but the jump alone is not evidence of one.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Why keyword match misses meaning and cross-encoders are too slow
question: You must rank 1,000,000 passages for each incoming query. Which cost profile describes a pure cross-encoder versus a bi-encoder at query time?
options: Both need 1,000,000 forward passes per query; the bi-encoder just uses a smaller model
Cross-encoder: 1,000,000 forward passes per query. Bi-encoder: 1 forward pass for the query plus 1,000,000 vector similarities
Cross-encoder: 1 forward pass per query. Bi-encoder: 1,000,000 forward passes
Both need 1 forward pass, because attention handles all passages at once
explain: The cross-encoder has to read the query together with every passage, so its work scales with the corpus on every query. The bi-encoder encoded the passages offline; online it encodes only the query and then does cheap dot products, which an index can speed up further.

courseTitle: Text embeddings and semantic search
lessonTitle: Where dense retrieval fails: hybrid search and re-ranking
question: In RRF with k = 60, document X is ranked 1st by BM25 and absent from the dense list. Document Y is ranked 3rd in both lists. Which ranks higher after fusion?
options: Y, because 2/63 is larger than 1/61
X, because a first place always wins
They tie
It depends on the raw BM25 score of X
explain: X gets 1/61, about 0.0164. Y gets 1/63 + 1/63, about 0.0317. RRF rewards agreement between retrievers, and it never looks at raw scores, so X's BM25 score is irrelevant.

courseTitle: Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)
lessonTitle: Byte-level BPE: how GPT-2 and its successors tokenize anything
question: The GPT-2 regex has no case-insensitive flag, and its source code carries a comment saying it should have had one. What does that cause for the text I'LL?
options: I'LL is one token
The contraction is not recognised: it splits as I | ' | LL
The regex lowercases it to i'll
It raises an error
explain: The contraction alternatives are lowercase ('ll, 're, ...), so 'LL does not match them. The apostrophe falls into the punctuation alternative and LL into the letters alternative, giving I, ', LL. The cl100k_base pattern wraps the contractions in a case-insensitive group.

courseTitle: Training deep nets in practice: init, optimizers, schedules, debugging
lessonTitle: Learning rate: the stability limit, warmup, decay and clipping
question: On $f(w) = 5w^2$, which learning rate converges fastest?
explain: Here h = 10, and the factor per step is 1 - 10 lr. At lr = 0.1 the factor is 0, so one step lands exactly at the minimum. 0.05 halves w each step, 0.19 oscillates with factor -0.9, and 0.21 diverges.

courseTitle: Vector search and ANN: how HNSW finds neighbors fast
lessonTitle: HNSW layers: a skip list made of graphs
question: A teammate sets m_L very high (for example 5) so the hierarchy is taller. What does the HNSW paper say happens when m_L is too large?
options: Recall drops to zero because layer 0 becomes empty
Memory shrinks because fewer links are stored
Neighbors overlap more across layers, so extra layers add little and search gets slower
Nothing changes; m_L only affects build time
explain: The paper explains that larger m_L means more overlap between layers (more nodes repeated on many layers), which hurts performance, while too small m_L increases the number of hops on each layer. That tradeoff is why it picks m_L = 1/ln M, matching a skip list with p = 1/M.

courseTitle: Synthetic data and model collapse
lessonTitle: Language models: decoding cuts the tail, scaling stalls
question: You generate 10x more synthetic training text from the same teacher with top-p 0.9. Under the tail-cutting model, when does this stop improving the student?
options: Never: error keeps falling as a power law in T
Once T exceeds roughly k to the power beta, where k is the effective tail cut; after that error plateaus at the missing tail mass
Immediately: synthetic data never helps
Only when the teacher's perplexity exceeds the student's
explain: Data from a tail-cut generator only teaches the head of the distribution. Once the student has learned the head, the remaining error is the mass of the items it never sees, and more samples from the same generator cannot reveal them.

courseTitle: System calls and mmap
lessonTitle: What a system call costs, and how to make fewer of them
question: A logger issues one `write` per 40-byte log line and handles 200,000 lines per second. Which change cuts syscall overhead the most?
options: Switch from write to pwrite
Accumulate lines in a 64 KiB buffer and write when it fills or on a short timer
Call fsync after every line so the kernel batches better
Open the log file with O_APPEND
explain: Overhead scales with the number of calls. Buffering 64 KiB packs about 1,638 lines per call, so 200,000 calls per second become about 122. pwrite and O_APPEND change semantics, not call count, and fsync adds an even more expensive call per line. Keep a flush timer so a crash or a quiet period does not hold lines forever.

courseTitle: Tail latency (p99, p99.9) and coordinated omission
lessonTitle: Coordinated omission: the load tester stops looking when it hurts
question: A closed-loop benchmark with 50 connections reports p99 = 4 ms. During the run the server had a 2 second GC pause. Which is the most likely truth?
options: p99 is about 4 ms; the pause produced at most 50 slow samples and those are correctly counted
The true p99 for users arriving at a constant rate is likely far higher, because requests that should have been sent during the pause were never sent or measured
p99 is lower than 4 ms because the pause reduced load
Percentiles are unaffected by coordinated omission; only the mean is
explain: Each of the 50 connections recorded one long sample during the pause and then nothing until it resumed. A constant-rate workload would have issued many requests during those 2 seconds, each waiting out the pause. Those are missing, so the reported p99 is biased low. wrk2's README shows a 1.4 s pause turning p99 from 6.04 ms (uncorrected) into 1.27 s.

courseTitle: Temporal reasoning: years of experience and current roles
lessonTitle: Why summing job durations overstates experience
question: Which single fact must be fixed before *current role* or *in the last 5 years* can be computed at all?
options: The candidate's time zone
The job titles of each role
The reference date that Present and now refer to
Whether the roles overlap
explain: Both questions are relative to a moment: current means containing that moment, and the last 5 years is a window ending at it. Without an explicit reference date the same resume gives different answers on different days.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Two ways to spend more compute on one prompt
question: A team samples 16 answers per question from a fixed model and keeps the one their reward model scores highest. In the proposer/verifier frame, what are they changing?
options: Only the verifier side: the proposal distribution is the same model sampled 16 times
Only the proposer: more samples means a better model
Both, because sampling at temperature changes the model's weights
Neither: this is training-time compute
explain: Best-of-N leaves the proposer untouched; each of the 16 samples comes from the same distribution. All the gain comes from selecting among them with a verifier. Changing the proposer means, for example, conditioning on previous attempts (revisions) or a longer reasoning trace.

courseTitle: Test-time compute scaling: sampling, search and thinking longer
lessonTitle: Thinking longer: reasoning models and budget forcing
question: You fine-tuned a model like s1 and force 10 extra "Wait" continuations on every hard problem. Accuracy drops compared with 4. What is the most likely cause?
options: The model forgot its fine-tuning
Too many suppressed stops push it into repetitive loops or past the context window, so extra tokens stop adding useful reasoning
Appending "Wait" changes the model's weights
Budget forcing only works on easy problems
explain: s1 reports that scaling with budget forcing flattens and that suppressing the end-of-thinking delimiter too often leads to repetitive loops, while the context window bounds total length.

courseTitle: Test-time training and learned memory: TTT layers and Titans
lessonTitle: Making TTT fast: mini-batch gradient descent and the dual form
question: You raise the TTT mini-batch size from 16 to 2048 in a TTT-Linear language model and change nothing else. What do you expect?
options: Lower perplexity, because larger batches give less noisy gradients
No change in quality; b is purely a speed knob because the dual form is exact
Faster training per step but worse perplexity, since the inner loop now takes far fewer real steps (b = T is batch GD, close to linear attention)
Slower training and better perplexity
explain: The dual form is exact for a given b, but b itself changes the algorithm. The TTT paper's ablation shows smaller b improves perplexity because W takes more gradient steps; b = T collapses to batch GD. LaCT gets away with huge chunks only by adding window attention, wider nonlinear fast weights and a different update rule.

courseTitle: Thread caches and magazines
lessonTitle: The magazine: a per-CPU stack of object pointers
question: Why does a magazine store an array of pointers instead of threading a linked list through the free objects themselves?
options: Arrays are always faster to traverse than linked lists
Writing a link into a free object would destroy its constructed state, and some managed resources are not writable memory
Linked lists cannot be used as stacks
The depot needs to sort the objects by address
explain: Object caches keep free objects in their constructed state (locks initialized, fields set). A freelist link would clobber part of the object. And the slab and magazine code also manage non-memory resources, where there is nowhere to store a link.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: Why memory is becoming a hierarchy of tiers
question: A service has 200 GB allocated, of which 40 GB is touched every few seconds and the rest is idle for minutes. Which configuration best fits tiered memory?
options: 64 GB DRAM and 160 GB CXL, with the OS demoting idle pages to CXL
160 GB DRAM and 40 GB CXL, so hot pages are guaranteed to fit
200 GB of CXL only, since CXL is cheaper per GB
64 GB DRAM and 160 GB of SSD swap, since swap is cheapest
explain: The hot 40 GB fits in 64 GB of DRAM with headroom, and idle pages go to cheaper CXL where they remain directly addressable. All-CXL puts hot data 2x farther away, and swap-only makes every access to a cold page a fault plus an SSD read.

courseTitle: Tiered memory: placing pages across DRAM, CXL and SSD
lessonTitle: The SSD tier, zswap, and running tiering in production
question: Why does TPP not use CXL memory as a fast swap device instead of a NUMA node?
options: Swap cannot be placed on byte-addressable memory
CXL devices do not support writes
Swap semantics turn every access into a major fault and a full-page copy, losing CXL's direct cache-line loads
The kernel cannot migrate pages to CXL
explain: The value of CXL is that warm pages can be read in place with a load at roughly 2x DRAM latency. Treating it as swap would add a fault and a 4 KiB copy to every access to a swapped page.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: From threads to blocks: the Triton programming model
question: A teammate moves a fused kernel from CUDA to Triton. Which of these do they still have to decide themselves in Triton?
options: Where to put __syncthreads() barriers between shared memory writes and reads
How large a tile each program instance processes and how the grid maps to tiles
Which thread in a warp loads which address so loads are coalesced
How much shared memory to allocate for staging operand tiles
explain: Tile sizes and the program-to-tile mapping are the programmer's job in Triton (often with the autotuner's help). Barriers, coalescing and shared memory allocation are listed in the Triton docs as things the compiler handles automatically.

courseTitle: Triton kernels: block-level GPU programming
lessonTitle: Autotuning, num_warps, num_stages and when to use Triton
question: A matmul config with BLOCK 128 x 256 x 64 in fp16 is extended from num_stages=3 to num_stages=6. Using the simplified estimate, what is the most likely result on a compute capability 9.0 GPU (228 KB of shared memory per SM, at most 227 KB per thread block)?
options: A 2x speedup because twice as many loads overlap
No change, because num_stages only affects registers
It needs about 288 KiB of operand buffers, more than the SM has, so the config fails to launch or is unusable
The compiler automatically shrinks the tiles to fit
explain: 6 x 49,152 bytes = 294,912 bytes (288 KiB) of operand buffers, beyond the 227 KB a thread block may use on compute capability 9.0. Even when stages fit, they help only while there is load latency left to hide; after that they just cost memory.

courseTitle: Unified multimodal models: one transformer that reads and draws
lessonTitle: Continuous images: one transformer, two losses
question: A Transfusion-style step has L_LM = 0.942 and L_DDPM = 0.07375. What is the total loss with lambda = 5?
explain: 0.942 + 5 x 0.07375 = 0.942 + 0.369 = 1.311. 1.016 is lambda = 1. 4.78 wrongly multiplies the text term by 5 instead (5 x 0.942 + 0.074 is about 4.78).

courseTitle: Unikernels: one application, one address space, one VM image
lessonTitle: Building the image: micro-libraries, configuration and dead code
question: A function-as-a-service platform boots a fresh nginx unikernel for each burst of requests and destroys it after a few seconds. Which allocator choice from the Unikraft measurements fits best?
options: A fast-booting allocator such as bootalloc, because boot time dominates a short-lived instance
The buddy allocator, because its throughput at steady state matched TLSF and mimalloc
Any allocator, because allocator choice only affects throughput
mimalloc, because it is always fastest
explain: For just-in-time instances, boot time matters most, and allocator choice moved nginx guest boot from 0.49 ms (bootalloc) to 3.07 ms (buddy). The paper itself says such a use case should avoid the buddy allocator.

courseTitle: Vector database internals: SIMD kernels, segments and disk
lessonTitle: SIMD distance kernels: lanes, FMA and the horizontal sum
question: A colleague's AVX-512 kernel uses one accumulator and runs 768-d distances on vectors that fit in L1. Splitting it into four accumulators makes it faster. Why?
options: Four accumulators halve the number of loads
Independent accumulators let several FMAs run in parallel instead of waiting on one dependency chain
AVX-512 cannot use a single register for more than 12 FMAs
Four accumulators avoid the horizontal sum
explain: Each FMA into the same register must wait for the previous result. Four independent chains keep the FMA units busy. Loads and the final reduction are unchanged (the reduction even gets slightly longer).

courseTitle: verl: the HybridFlow RL training stack for LLMs
lessonTitle: WorkerGroups, resource pools and DataProto dispatch
question: `init_model` is registered with Dispatch.ONE_TO_ALL. What does the controller send to each worker when it calls `wg.init_model()`?
options: A different slice of the arguments to each worker
The same arguments, replicated once per worker
Arguments only to rank 0, which then broadcasts them
Nothing; ONE_TO_ALL methods run on the controller process
explain: dispatch_one_to_all copies every argument world_size times, so every worker runs the same call. It suits setup methods like init_model. DP_COMPUTE_PROTO is the mode that splits a DataProto into per-worker chunks.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Why an hour of video does not fit: frames times tokens
question: A team doubles the frame rate from 1 fps to 2 fps and also switches from 196 to 49 tokens per frame. What happens to the total token count for the same video?
options: It doubles
It halves
It stays the same
It drops to a quarter
explain: Total = frames x tokens per frame. Frames go up 2x, tokens per frame go down 4x (196 to 49), so the total is 2/4 = 0.5 of the original. More temporal detail can be bought with less spatial detail.

courseTitle: Video-LLMs with long-video memory
lessonTitle: Merging similar frames: MovieChat and MA-LMM memory banks
question: MovieChat's short-term memory holds 18 frames of 32 tokens and consolidates to 2 frames. How many visual tokens does each consolidation add to long-term memory?
explain: 2 frames x 32 tokens = 64 tokens. The 18 x 32 = 576 tokens in the buffer shrink 9x, and long-term memory is capped at 256 frames, 8,192 tokens.

courseTitle: Video world models: Genie, latent actions and neural game engines
lessonTitle: Latent actions: a controller learned from unlabelled video
question: Which part of the latent action model is still used when a person plays Genie?
options: The encoder, to infer actions from the player's screen
The decoder, to render each frame
Only the VQ codebook, indexed by the integer the player chooses
Nothing; the dynamics model takes raw keyboard codes
explain: Apart from the VQ codebook, the entire LAM is discarded at inference. The player's integer in [0, 8) selects a code vector, whose embedding conditions the dynamics model.

courseTitle: Fine-tuning a vision model (ViT)
lessonTitle: Where ViT-B/16's 86 million parameters live
question: You switch from 224x224 to 384x384 inputs on ViT-B/16. Which parameter tensor has to change shape?
options: Every Q, K and V matrix, because the sequence is longer
The patch projection E, because there are more patches
Only the position embedding table, from 197 x 768 to 577 x 768
None: the model handles any resolution without changes
explain: Attention and MLP weights act on each token's D-vector, so their shapes depend on D, not on sequence length. E acts on each 16x16x3 patch, unchanged. Only the learned table has one row per slot, so it must grow from 197 to 577 rows.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: From a VLM that describes to a VLA that acts
question: In Open X-Embodiment, two robots receive the identical 7-number action vector. Why might they move very differently?
options: The 256-bin tokenizer uses a different vocabulary for each robot
Actions are normalized per dataset and frames and control modes (position vs velocity, absolute vs relative) are not aligned, so the same numbers mean different motions
Open X-Embodiment stores only images, so actions are re-estimated per robot
The model adds a robot-specific noise term at inference
explain: The paper says the alignment is coarse: each dataset's actions are normalized separately and coordinate frames are not aligned, so an output is de-normalized differently per embodiment and the same vector can induce very different motions.

courseTitle: Vision-language-action models: RT-2, OpenVLA and pi0
lessonTitle: Running action chunks in the control loop
question: In ACT's temporal ensemble, you lower m from 0.5 to 0.01. What changes?
options: Only the oldest prediction is used
Weights become nearly equal, so newer predictions count about as much as old ones and new observations are incorporated faster
The ensemble becomes a median instead of a mean
The policy is queried less often
explain: With m near 0, exp(-m i) is close to 1 for every i, so all predictions are averaged almost equally. The ACT paper states that a smaller m means faster incorporation of new observations.

courseTitle: Visual tokenizers: turning images into discrete tokens
lessonTitle: Codebook collapse: measuring and fixing unused codes
question: Why does a dead code stay dead under the plain VQ-VAE codebook loss?
options: Its gradient is clipped by the commitment term
It receives gradient only when it is the nearest code to some encoder output, which it never is
The straight-through estimator sends it the wrong sign
Its distance is always zero
explain: The codebook term only involves the chosen code e_k. A code that never wins the argmin gets zero gradient, so it never moves toward the data and keeps losing.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: One attention layer, many kernels: the backend abstraction
question: A model has 32 attention layers that all use the same backend and one KV cache group. In one engine step, how many times does that backend's metadata builder run `build()`?
options: Once, and all 32 layers reuse the result
32 times, once per layer, because each layer has its own KV cache
Once per request in the batch
Zero times on decode steps, because decode metadata is cached
explain: The builder runs once per step per KV cache group, and the layers in that group share the metadata object. Per-layer work happens in `AttentionImpl.forward`. That is why `forward` must stay cheap on the CPU.

courseTitle: vLLM attention backends: selection, batching, KV layout, CUDA graphs
lessonTitle: CUDA graphs: padding, support levels and mode downgrades
question: With `max_num_seqs = 256` (max capture size 512), which batch wastes the largest *fraction* of its padded graph?
options: 257 tokens
100 tokens
9 tokens
511 tokens
explain: 9 pads to 16, wasting 7 of 16 rows (43.8%). 257 pads to 272 (5.5%), 100 to 104 (3.8%) and 511 to 512 (0.2%). Small batches matter most for latency, which is why `performance_mode = interactivity` captures every size from 1 to 32.

courseTitle: Vision-language models for reading images
lessonTitle: What an image costs: provider token formulas and resizing rules
question: You must read 6 pt text on scanned invoices with an OpenAI model that uses the tile rule. Which choice best protects accuracy?
options: Set detail to low to save tokens
Send the full 4000 px scan and trust the model
Crop the text region (or split the page) so that after the 768 px shortest-side rule the text stays legible
Convert the image to grayscale
explain: With the tile rule a big page is shrunk until its shortest side is 768 px, which can make small print illegible. Low detail is even coarser. Cropping or splitting keeps more pixels per character.

courseTitle: Wait-free algorithms: bounded progress for every thread
lessonTitle: A practical wait-free queue: phases and helping (Kogan-Petrank)
question: Thread 1's enqueue was linearized by a helper, but a different helper is still suspended between marking thread 1 not pending and swinging tail. Thread 1 returns immediately and starts a new operation. What does the paper say goes wrong if `enq()` skips its final `help_finish_enq()` call?
options: Nothing, because tail is only a hint
The node is enqueued twice
Thread 1's next dequeue returns the wrong value
Further enqueues can be blocked until the suspended helper resumes, which breaks wait-freedom
explain: help_finish_enq checks that the owner's descriptor still points at the dangling node. Once thread 1 has published a new descriptor that check fails, so no one fixes tail and every later enqueue waits on the suspended helper. The final call ensures tail is past your node before you return.

courseTitle: Weather and climate foundation models: GraphCast to Aurora
lessonTitle: Rolling a 6-hour step out to 10 days
question: A team trains a 6-hour model only on single-step targets and finds its 10-day rollouts drift badly. Which fix is GraphCast's approach?
options: Train on 1-hour steps so each step is easier
Add more layers so the single-step error goes to zero
Use an L1 loss instead of MSE
Backpropagate a loss over several autoregressive steps, growing the number of steps during training
explain: GraphCast's loss covers N rollout steps, increased from 1 to 12, so the model sees its own outputs as inputs during training. Shorter steps mean more calls and more accumulated error (Pangu's finding), and no network reaches zero one-step error.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Why a pool needs more than one shared queue
question: A pool runs 8 workers on 2 us tasks, and its single locked queue costs 0.5 us of serialized work per task. Using the lesson's model, about how many workers can the queue keep busy?
options: All 8, since 2 us tasks are much longer than 0.5 us
About 5, since (s + c)/c = 2.5/0.5 = 5
About 2, since only one thread can hold the lock
About 4, since half the time is spent in the queue
explain: The queue hands out at most 1/c = 2 tasks per us, and each worker consumes 1/(s+c) = 0.4 tasks per us, so the queue saturates at 2/0.4 = 5 workers. The other 3 mostly wait on the lock.

courseTitle: Work stealing and thread pools
lessonTitle: Parking idle workers without lost wakeups or thundering herds
question: A Tokio runtime has 8 workers and 4 of them are currently searching. A fifth idle worker tries to start searching. What happens?
options: It starts searching; there is no limit
It wakes all other parked workers first
It is refused, because 2 x 4 >= 8, so it goes back to parking
It steals from the global queue only
explain: transition_worker_to_searching returns false when 2 x num_searching >= num_workers, so at most about half the workers search at once. Tokio calls the limit sloppy on purpose: it is a throttle, not an exact bound.

courseTitle: WSD learning-rate schedules
lessonTitle: Tuning the cooldown: length, shape, floor and data
question: Why can 1-sqrt beat linear for the same cooldown length?
options: It reaches low LR earlier in the cooldown, giving more steps for the bouncing to settle, at the cost of a little river progress
It keeps the LR near peak for longer during the cooldown
It never reaches zero, so the model keeps learning
It is identical to cosine to 10%
explain: Halfway through the cooldown 1-sqrt is at 0.293 of peak versus 0.5 for linear. Its average LR over the cooldown is 1/3 versus 1/2, so it gives up some area (river progress) in exchange for more time at small LR to shrink the hill part.

courseTitle: Zero-copy I/O: sendfile, splice and MSG_ZEROCOPY
lessonTitle: splice and tee: pipes as buffers of page references
question: Which call fails with EINVAL?
options: splice(file_fd, &off, pipe_w, NULL, n, 0)
splice(sock_fd, NULL, pipe_w, NULL, n, SPLICE_F_NONBLOCK)
tee(pipe1_r, pipe2_w, n, 0)
splice(file_fd, &off, sock_fd, NULL, n, 0)
explain: splice requires that at least one side is a pipe; file to socket has none, so it returns EINVAL. For file to socket use sendfile, which builds the internal pipe for you. The other three each involve a pipe on the correct side.

courseTitle: Zero-shot classification: labels chosen at inference time
lessonTitle: Embedding similarity with label descriptions
question: For T1 with descriptions, raising the softmax scale from 20 to 100 changes complaint's probability from 0.978 to about 1.0. What happens to accuracy?
options: It rises, because the model is more confident
It falls, because the model becomes overconfident
It does not change: scaling all cosines by the same factor keeps the ranking, so the argmax is identical
It depends on the embedding dimension
explain: Multiplying every cosine by the same positive number preserves their order, so the top label is unchanged for every input. Only the reported confidence changes, which is why softmax outputs from a hand-picked scale should not be read as calibrated probabilities.
